items.titleOriginal: Παγκόσμια πρωταθλήτρια στο τραμπολίνο η Αλεξάνδρα Εφραίμογλου στην Κίνα
items.description: Η ιστορία γράφτηκε στο Παγκόσμιο Πρωτάθλημα Τραμπολίνο που πραγματοποιείται στο Ναντζίνγκ της Κίνας, καθώς για πρώτη φορά δύο Ελληνίδες αθλήτριες εξασφάλισαν την πρόκρισή τους στον τελικό του Ατομικού Ακροβατικού Διαδρόμου, επιβεβαιώνοντας τη δυναμική και την αγωνιστική εξέλιξη του ελληνικού αθλήματος. Και η συνέχεια ήταν ακόμη πιο εντυπωσιακή… Η Αλεξάνδρα Εφραίμογλου ανέβηκε στο ψηλότερο…
items.descriptionOriginal: Η ιστορία γράφτηκε στο Παγκόσμιο Πρωτάθλημα Τραμπολίνο που πραγματοποιείται στο Ναντζίνγκ της Κίνας, καθώς για πρώτη φορά δύο Ελληνίδες αθλήτριες εξασφάλισαν την πρόκρισή τους στον τελικό του Ατομικού Ακροβατικού Διαδρόμου, επιβεβαιώνοντας τη δυναμική και την αγωνιστική εξέλιξη του ελληνικού αθλήματος. Και η συνέχεια ήταν ακόμη πιο εντυπωσιακή… Η Αλεξάνδρα Εφραίμογλου ανέβηκε στο ψηλότερο σκαλί του βάθρου, κατακτώντας το χρυσό μετάλλιο και τον τίτλο της Παγκόσμιας Πρωταθλήτριας, ενώ η Μαρία Αριστείδου πραγματοποίησε εξαιρετική εμφάνιση, καταλαμβάνοντας την 6η θέση στον κόσμο. Δύο Ελληνίδες στον παγκόσμιο τελικό, ένα χρυσό μετάλλιο και μια ακόμη σπουδαία παρουσία στην κορυφαία εξάδα του κόσμου. Μια διάκριση που αποτελεί ορόσημο για το ελληνικό Τραμπολίνο και ανοίγει νέους ορίζοντες για το μέλλον του αθλήματος στη χώρα μας. Η ΕΓΟ συνεχάρη τις δύο αθλήτριες γράφοντας στην επίσημη ιστοσελίδα της: «Θερμά συγχαρητήρια στην Αλεξάνδρα και τη Μαρία, στους προπονητές τους, αλλά και σε όλους όσοι εργάζονται καθημερινά για την ανάπτυξη και την πρόοδο της ελληνικής Γυμναστικής». Από την πλευρά της η Ελληνική Ολυμπιακή Επιτροπή (ΕΟΕ) προέβη στην εξής ανάρτηση στο “Χ”: «Tεράστια επιτυχία για το ελληνικό Τραμπολίνο και για την Ελληνική Γυμναστική! H Aλεξάνδρα Εφραίμογλου κατέκτησε το χρυσό μετάλλιο στο Παγκόσμιο Πρωτάθλημα Τραμπολίνο στο Ναντζίνγκ της Κίνας. Θερμά συγχαρητήρια Αλεξάνδρα». Ο αναπληρωτής Υπουργός Αθλητισμού Γιάννης Βρούτσης επισήμανε στην ανάρτησή του στο “Χ”: Στην κορυφή του κόσμου η Aλεξάνδρα Εφραίμογλου. Η 22χρονη Πρωταθλήτρια Ευρώπης κατέκτησε το χρυσό μετάλλιο και στο Παγκόσμιο Πρωτάθλημα Τραμπολίνο, στον ακροβατικό διάδρομο. Θερμά συγχαρητήρια, Αλεξάνδρα, πολλά μπράβο σε προπονητές & Ομοσπονδία Γυμναστικής www.ertnews.gr

items.descriptionOriginal: They say New York City is the City of Dreams. Young people all over the world flock to the city when they’re ready to start chasing after their biggest ambitions. If you have a passion for theater, television, or the arts, there’s no better place to be. Want to become a successful and prestigious stock broker, lawyer, or investment banker? It’s all New York , baby. It’s a city of immense opportunity and tough competition, but that’s what makes it full of life and culture for those who choose to live there. But all of that doesn’t come cheap. The average rent in New York for even just a small, studio apartment is now over $4,000 per month. That buys you less than 500 square feet. And, even though it seems like you’re really pinching pennies by living somewhere so cramped, that price tag is enormous! Even if you account for the higher-than-average salaries in New York. Most young people just getting started in their careers can’t afford that. Not to mention, the competition for good-quality apartments in New York is cutthroat. Still, people are desperate to live there by any means necessary, which has given rise to some really fascinating (and, in some cases, slightly horrifying) micro apartments. Meet the woman behind the viral apartment In 2022, one woman went viral for showing off her New York micro apartment. It clocks in at just 80 square feet and cost her, at the time, a meager $650 per month. Creator Caleb Simpson interviewed the woman, Alaina Randazzo, for his series that specializes in featuring interesting and unique living spaces. Alaina’s apartment definitely qualifies. “So really it just feels like a walk-in closet,” Simpson remarks upon entering through the front door. Alaina shows Simpson around the apartment, which includes a tiny living room slash kitchen area with a mini-fridge, a small sink, and a small stove and microwave. In the main living area, she’s placed a fold-out sofa of sorts. Alaina’s makeup and pantry foods are all crammed into one small cabinet. From there… well, there’s not much left to see. But Alaina and Simpson check out the loft, which holds Alaina’s bed and a little extra storage in the form of hooks where she hangs her bags and purses. The apartment has no windows, only a skylight above the loft bed.. There is a storage cupboard under the stairs, but it’s hard to access. “Every time I want to get something out, something else has to move,” Alaina says. As far as a bathroom, Alaina is lucky enough to have her very own private bathroom complete with shower! Many New York micro apartments feature communal or shared bathrooms, so the private bath is a plus for this tiny space. However, hers is located separate from her apartment, down the hall. And, you might be surprised to hear, it’s extremely tiny. Inside the 80-square-foot apartment Alaina admits she previously lived in a “luxury” apartment that cost over $3,000 per month, but she wanted to free up money to travel, which prompted her to downgrade. Watch the whole tour here: Alaina says her tiny apartment was a “hot commodity” when she signed the lease, beating out tons of other prospective renters. The internet had a lot to say about it Commenters on the video, which has racked up millions of views, were more or less horrified at the conditions that New Yorkers were competing over: “Firetrap . No exits , no windows with fresh air . Cooking with no air flow . Crazy this is even happening” “I can’t even breathe looking at this tiny apartment” “‘In a van, down by the river’ has never sounded better.” “NYC should be ashamed and embarrassed to relegate people to live in this kind of space. Not only does it look uncomfortable / unhealthy but It looks extremely dangerous. NYC should do better in providing affordable housing with decent square footage.” It’s cool and scrappy that Alaina makes the pint-sized apartment work for her as she pursues her dream of living in New York City. We might find it claustrophobic, but the fact that multiple renters were fighting over this space really says a lot about the way our culture is moving. Why she’s not chasing the picket fence Many younger millennials and Gen Z are sick of chasing after the American Dream of the single-family home with a white picket fence and a golden retriever. It’s hopelessly out of reach for many of them anyway due to skyrocketing housing prices and stagnant wages. So, they can work their fingers to the bone with multiple jobs and maybe afford a slightly better apartment, but still not be able to save enough for the future, or they could actually enjoy their life with the money they do have. NBC News reported in 2024, “Several years out of Covid lockdowns, younger Americans’ outlays on things like travel, recreation and dining out have been outpacing their older peers’ even as the economy slows. As of the summer of 2023, the average Gen Zer or millennial was dropping over $400 a month on nonessentials, compared to about $250 for Gen Xers and less than $200 for baby boomers.” In another YouTube interview, Alaina admits to spending big money on her monthly gym membership: over $300 per month, to be exact. Commenters chastised her for having her priorities mixed up, but honestly, there’s nothing backwards at all about wanting to relax at your gym’s spa after a long day of work, or travel to the far ends of the world, versus spending all of your money on an OK-but-still-cramped apartment. In an update in the YouTube video’s caption, Simpson writes that Alaina chose not to renew her lease in the micro apartment after filming. But that doesn’t mean she regrets her stay. “It’s an adventure,” Alaina says. “People need a lot less than they think they need.” This article originally appeared last year. It has been updated. The post Woman gives tour of her $650 New York micro apartment and people were unprepared appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: Agatha Christie is widely celebrated as one of the best-selling authors in history . She penned more than 80 books, selling billions of copies worldwide. Her intricate detective plots and brilliant murder mysteries have captivated readers for over a century. However, few people realize that her meticulous attention to detail didn’t just entertain readers; it actually saved a dying child’s life . In June 1977, a 19-month-old girl was flown from Qatar to London in critical condition. She was admitted to Hammersmith Hospital suffering from a severe, cascading illness that completely baffled the medical staff. The toddler was semi-conscious, her blood pressure was dangerously low, she had immense difficulty breathing, and her hair had begun to fall out in clumps. Doctors ran a battery of tests for rare disorders, but every lead turned into a dead end as her condition continued to rapidly decline. The breakthrough didn’t come from a medical journal. It came from a paperback novel. A nurse spots a clue in her novel A nurse named Marsha Maitland was caring for the little girl while reading Christie’s 1961 crime novel The Pale Horse . In the book, characters fall victim to a mysterious illness whose most distinctive symptom is hair falling out, a classic sign of thallium poisoning. The description struck Maitland. She looked at the toddler in the bed, noticed the identical symptom, and began to wonder if life was imitating art. The next morning, Maitland presented her theory to the attending physician. Dr. Victor Dubowitz, a professor of pediatrics at the Royal Postgraduate Medical School , admitted that the staff was “in a state where almost any suggestion was welcome,” as reported by The Washington Post . Because thallium poisoning was incredibly rare in Britain at the time, the hospital lacked the specialized equipment needed to test for it. Desperate for answers, Dubowitz contacted Scotland Yard to locate a laboratory capable of running a toxicity screen. In a bizarre twist, Scotland Yard also put the medical team in touch with a thallium expert who was serving time at Wormwood Scrubs Prison and happened to possess detailed notes on the chemical’s effects. When the toxicology results finally came back, the lab confirmed that the little girl had 10 times the lethal level of thallium in her system. Investigators later discovered that the chemical had been used as a pesticide to control cockroaches and rodents in her family’s home in Qatar. With the source of the illness identified, doctors immediately began the correct treatment. Within three weeks, the child showed “remarkable” improvement, and four months later, she was discharged to return home with her parents. “When we last saw her, she had made a good deal of progress and was sitting up and taking notice again,” Dubowitz recalled. How Christie knew her poisons Christie’s uncanny ability to describe the poisoning so accurately was rooted in her real-world experience. According to historian Lucy Worsley, author of the biography Agatha Christie: An Elusive Woman , Christie’s path to detective fiction solidified during World War I, when she moved from working in hospital wards to the dispensary. “This was the tipping point,” Worsley told ABC News Australia, explaining that the job required mixing precise medicinal formulations by hand. It was in that dispensary that Christie acquired a profound, clinical knowledge of lethal compounds, giving her an expertise that, decades later, would jump off the page to guide a nurse and save a little girl’s life. This article originally appeared in July. It has been updated. The post Doctors couldn’t identify what was killing a baby in 1977 until a nurse remembered a line from an Agatha Christie book appeared first on Upworthy .

items.titleOriginal: Hair salons in Europe are dumping their clippings into forests and it’s miraculous
items.description: Κάθε μέρα, τα κομμωτήρια σκουπίζουν αμέτρητα αποκομμένα μαλλιά από το πάτωμά τους και τα πετούν στα σκουπίδια χωρίς πολλή σκέψη. Η γαλλική εταιρεία ανακύκλωσης Capillum έχει αναπτύξει έναν εκπληκτικά αποτελεσματικό τρόπο επαναχρησιμοποίησης του χούμα…
items.descriptionOriginal: Every day, hair salons sweep countless hair clippings off their floors and toss them into the trash without much thought. But in parts of France, Belgium, and Luxembourg, those discarded strands are finding an entirely different purpose: helping forests grow. French recycling company Capillum has developed a surprisingly effective way to reuse human hair by turning it into biodegradable mulch that protects young trees from hungry deer. The company collects hair from participating salons and transforms it into flattened fiber sheets that can be wrapped around vulnerable saplings. What sounds unusual at first actually solves several environmental problems at once. A second life for salon clippings Hair salons generate an enormous amount of waste each year. Most clippings are simply thrown away, even though human hair is remarkably durable because it is made largely from keratin, a fibrous protein that breaks down slowly over time. Capillum saw potential in a material most people never think twice about. The company accepts hair regardless of texture, length, color, or whether it has been dyed. Once gathered, the hair is fed into a machine that minces everything together into dense fiber sheets that can be laid around the base of trees. The process transforms something typically viewed as garbage into a practical tool for conservation efforts. Why young trees need protection A group of people planting saplings. Photo credit: Canva Many forests depend on saplings surviving long enough to mature and replenish the ecosystem. However, young trees often struggle in areas with large deer populations. Deer are known to chew on bark, especially during seasons when food is scarce. Because saplings have thin bark and delicate trunks, even small amounts of damage can stunt their growth or kill them entirely. Foresters have historically relied on plastic fencing and tree guards to keep deer away. While those barriers can work well, they also create waste and require maintenance over time. Capillum’s recycled hair mats offer another approach. The scent of human hair naturally discourages deer from getting too close to the trees, steering them toward other vegetation instead. The method protects saplings without harming wildlife. How the hair mulch gives back to soil Unlike plastic guards, the hair fibers gradually decompose and return nutrients to the soil. As the keratin breaks down, it releases nitrogen and other nutrients that can support plant growth. That nutrient-rich quality is one reason some gardeners have long experimented with placing hair into compost piles or using it directly in garden beds. Capillum also sells its eco-friendly hair mulch to home gardeners interested in more sustainable growing methods. This is far from the first time Capillum has found creative uses for human hair. The company is also developing hair-based absorbents designed to soak up oil and other hydrocarbons from water and soil. Around the world, scientists and environmental groups have similarly explored using recycled hair for oil spill cleanup, agricultural mats, and composting projects. Some studies have even examined whether hair fibers could eventually help create insulation materials or textiles. All this to say: a routine haircut may not seem connected to forest conservation, yet the thousands of discarded strands now helping protect young trees suggest otherwise. This is a brilliant example of humanity using creativity for good, and how making just one element of human life less wasteful can have a profound impact. This article originally appeared in May. It has been updated. The post Hair salons in Europe are dumping their clippings into forests and it’s miraculous appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: It turns out “the voice of a generation ” isn’t just a metaphor. Different generations have different ways of speaking, and nowhere is it more obvious than in our television, commercials , and other pop culture. Even more interestingly, the way people talk in these cultural artifacts sometimes says more about culture in general than the way real people actually speak. For example, the classic “old-timey” accent you hear in films and radio from the early to mid-1900s, called Good American Speech or the Transatlantic accent, wasn’t exactly a reflection of how real people talked. It was adopted by actors to sound more refined and elite, but it’s how many of us often remember the period sounding. So, too, do modern Millennials have their own distinct voice. And one voice artist says it’s all Jim Halpert’s fault. The origins of Millennial speak Voice artist Tawny Platis has lent her vocal talents to Hulu, Warner Bros., Disney+, and many more. She also creates content online and shared a fascinating bit of history from her unique industry in a video. “Jim from The Office is responsible for the Millennial voice,” she proclaims. In order to explain why actor John Krasinski is the reason “Millennials talk like that,” she takes us back to the popular TV commercials of our youth. Brands like Macy’s and PetSmart would feature voiceover actors with a bright, cheery, in-your-face “commercial” voice. Platis performs them perfectly in her video because, she says, she actually starred in many commercials just like these. But before Krasinski made it big with his role on The Office , he was a prominent voice actor for brands like Verizon and Blackberry. In those commercials, many of which aired in the early 2000s and 2010s, he was famous for his extraordinarily casual, conversational tone. Think his laid-back Jim Halpert vibe. It’s a stark contrast to the way commercials were performed in the ’90s. “It was basically just like, ‘Hey, I’m just a guy. I’m not really an actor. … You can trust me. It’s like you’re talking to a friend.’” Platis says. Platis says that for years, until very recently, almost every audition and job she went out for was seeking a “conversational read” exactly like Krasinski’s performances. They became genre-defining. Hallmarks of Millennial voice explained Platis isn’t the first person to identify this distinct way of speaking. For years, “Millennial speak” has been examined (and sometimes maligned) in popular media. In 2016, NPR wrote about Millennials’ love of tacking on “I feel like” to their thoughts, a habit critics say avoids confrontation. Millennials are also famous for vocal fry, which the University of Melbourne describes as “the creaky voice they often do at the end of sentences that makes them sound eternally bored, cool and relaxed, depending on the listener.” The style of speaking reflected a powerful move away from anything that felt cheesy, artificial, or overly formal. For example, remember the “movie trailer voice” guy? Movie trailers don’t use those big, over-the-top narrators with deep gravitas anymore, preferring to let the footage and music speak for itself. This is partly due to the death of legendary voiceover man Don LaFontaine in 2008, but the movie trailer voiceover was also becoming too cliché and predictable for the Millennial audience. Krasinski, who’s naturally likable and “cool,” was the perfect person to bring all of this to life in his super chill but still-friendly way of speaking. It was only further cemented by the huge popularity of his character on The Office . Something changed in recent years Platis goes on to say that the Golden Age of Millennial Voice has come and gone, and Gen Zers are taking center stage in the voiceover world. She describes Gen Z voice as detached and apathetic, “like you’re talking to someone without looking up from your phone.” And it’s what all the brands want now. Interestingly, Platis says that the Gen Z voice more closely resembles the sarcasm and unbotheredness of Gen X, or their parents. In other words, it all comes back around. No matter what generation you come from, it’s all but certain that the next one will want to do things their own way . It can hurt to feel like pop culture is leaving you behind, but it’s a necessary process for young people to form their own identities as they take a leading role in the world. As far as Millennials go, though, that trademarked Jim Halpert voice will never go out of style. This article originally appeared in April. It has been updated. items.title: Το αίτημα της γυναίκας για «προτάσεις που αλλάζουν τη ζωή» είναι ένα χρυσωρυχείο σοφίας
items.titleOriginal: Woman’s request for ‘life-changing sentences’ is a gold mine of wisdom
items.description: Μερικές φορές, μια απλή φράση ή πρόταση σοφής συμβουλής μπορεί να έχει τεράστιο αντίκτυπο στη ζωή μας, είτε προέρχεται από ένα θρησκευτικό κείμενο, είτε από έναν ειδικό ψυχικής υγείας, είτε από ένα παλιό ρητό που έζησε η γιαγιά σας. Η Chelsea Anderson, μια δημιουργός περιεχομένου στο Ντένβερ του Κολοράντο, λατρεύει να συλλέγει αυτά τα μαργαριτάρια σοφίας, γι' αυτό ζήτησε από τους οπαδούς της στο TikTok να μοιραστούν το δικό τους…
items.descriptionOriginal: Sometimes, a simple phrase or sentence of sagely advice can have a huge impact on our lives, whether it’s from a religious text , a mental health expert, or an old saying your grandmother lived by. Chelsea Anderson , a content creator in Denver, Colorado , loves to collect these pearls of wisdom , so she asked her TikTok followers to share their favorite “life-changing sentences,” and they delivered by the thousands. Anderson is a popular figure on Instagram and TikTok for what began as babysitting life hacks, but she’s since graduated to becoming someone who “explains it all,” a playful riff on the 1990s sitcom Clarissa Explains It All . “I collect life-changing sentences,” she said in the video. “You know, something that you read and you’re just like, wow, this changes everything. I’m gonna give you some of mine, and then I wanna hear yours.” @chelseaexplainsitall I will compile the best ones and make another video! #quotes #inspiration ♬ original sound – ChelseaExplainsItAll Her life-changing sentences of wisdom “Growth can feel like grief when you loved who you were.” “The only way to discover all of the talents that you have within you is to give yourself permission to be a beginner.” “Don’t worry about disappointing people who do not impress you.” The most popular piece of wisdom: “Unspoken expectations are premeditated resentments.” This quote is commonly attributed to Neil Strauss , author of books including The Game and The Truth . The message is pretty simple: if you expect something from someone and never tell them, the other person has no chance to meet that expectation, which can inevitably lead to resentment. A woman at peace. Photo credit: Canva More words of wisdom Here are some more quotes that might help you find balance in everyday life. Quotes about life choices “People only see the choice you made, not the choices you had.” “The best time to plant a tree was 20 years ago, the second-best time is now.” “Twenty minutes of doing something is more valuable than 20 hours of thinking about doing something.” “Birds do not land on branches because they are certain the branch will hold. They land because they trust their wings to carry them if it doesn’t. Trust your wings.” “Easy and hard are just familiar and unfamiliar.” “You’ll never feel ready. Ready isn’t a feeling, it’s a decision.” “I trust the next chapter because I know the author.” A woman making a choice. Photo credit: Canva Quotes about relationships “Forgiveness is for mistakes, not patterns.” There is no clear origin for this phrase, but it has become a popular meme in recent years. The phrase matters because it’s about setting fair boundaries. We all make mistakes, but when there is a pattern of behavior the other person can’t seem to break, you shouldn’t give your forgiveness so easily. Eventually, it becomes enabling. “Over-explaining is a form of begging.” “You don’t have to attend every fight you are invited to.” “Sometimes the things that break your heart fix your vision.” “Never miss anyone who knows how to find you.” “Accept people as they are and place them where they belong.” “Don’t work harder than the person you’re helping.” Quotes about society “If you’re not allowed to question it, you’re being controlled by it.“ This quote offers a way of looking at the authoritarian forces in our lives. Whether it’s the government, the educational system, law enforcement, religion, the media, or even people in your family, when you’re not allowed to be critical or ask questions, those in authority are more interested in controlling you than serving you. “Equality can feel like oppression to the ones who have held power.” Quotes about mental health “You can’t hate yourself into a version of yourself you love.” This quote is often attributed to Lori Deschene , the founder of Tiny Buddha . She’s also the author of Tiny Buddha’s Gratitude Journal , Tiny Buddha’s Worry Journal , and more. The quote highlights the idea that self-improvement is more likely to come from self-acceptance than from self-criticism. “If it doesn’t change my life, then it shouldn’t change my mood.” “Avoidance is just prolonged suffering disguised as safety.” “People of value don’t go around devaluing others.” “You are not the voice in your head, you are the one that hears it.” Wisdom worth keeping in your pocket There’s something wonderful about having little pieces of wisdom in your back pocket that you can draw on whenever things get rough. Kudos to Anderson, who asked her audience to share the wisdom many people may really need right now. This article originally appeared in March. It has been updated. The post Woman’s request for ‘life-changing sentences’ is a gold mine of wisdom appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: Την 5η σερί νίκη του πανηγύρισε ο Άρης, περνώντας και από τη Λευκάδα, με 88-77, απέναντι στη Δόξα, στο πλαίσιο της 6ης αγωνιστικής της Greek Basketball League. Η ομάδα της Θεσσαλονίκης, μετά τη μεγάλη νίκη επί του Παναθηναϊκού στην 5η αγωνιστική, δεν βρήκε εμπόδιο στο νησί του Ιονίου, αυξάνοντας σε 5-1το ρεκόρ της. Τέσσερις παίκτες του Βασίλη Σπανούλη σημείωσαν διψήφιο νούμερο πόντων, με πρώτο σκόρερ ν’ αναδεικνύεται ο Νέναντ Ντιμιτρίεβιτς με 25 πόντους και 6/6 τρίποντα (!), 5 ασίστ και 4 ριμπάουντ. Λιντέλ και Ρόμπινσον-υπερίσχυσαν στη ρακέτα, προσθέτοντας 14 πόντους και 8 ριμπάουντ, όπως και 17 πόντους και 7 ριμπάουντ αντίστοιχα.Από τη Δόξα, η οποία υποχώρησε στο 2-4, ξεχώρισαν οι Χάρμον και Γκαντ με 22 και 18 πόντους αντίστοιχα. Τα δεκάλεπτα: 23-32, 35-51, 54-68, 77-88 Ο Άρης ήταν κυρίαρχος από την έναρξη του αγώνα και κατάφερε να προηγηθεί με +9 πόντους στο τέλος της 1ης περιόδου (23-32) χάρη στην κυριαρχία του Κώστα Αντετοκούνμπο στη ρακέτα και τα τρίποντα του Ντιμιτρίεβιτς. Οι Θεσσαλονικείς μπήκαν με επιμέρους σκορ 3-11 στη 2η περίοδο, με τους γηπεδούχους ν’ αδυνατούν ν’ ακολουθήσουν. Ο Άρης είχε ποιοτική διαφορά, είχε και τον Θανάση Αντετοκούνμπο να βγάζει άμυνες για… σεμινάριο και πήγε στ’ αποδυτήρια στο ημίχρονο με +16 υπέρ του διαφορά (35-51). Στο τρίτο δεκάλεπτο, Χάρμον και Γκραντ, έβαλαν δύσκολα στον Άρη, αλλά ο Ρόμπινσον-Ερλ γινόταν αποδέκτης της μπάλας στη ρακέτα και νικώντας κατά κράτος τους αντιπάλους του επέτρεψε στην ομάδα της Λευκάδας να πλησιάσει έως το 54-68, σκορ 3ης περιόδου. Ο Ντιμιτρίεβιτς παρέμεινε συνδεδεμένος με το καλάθι και στην 4η περίοδο και ο Άρης έφτασε άνετα στην 5η σερί νίκη του (88-77). Διαιτητές: Μαρινάκης, Μπακάλης, Ζαχαρής ΔΟΞΑ ΛΕΥΚΑΔΑΣ (Τερζής): Χάρμον 22, Πάρις 9 (2), Αρσενόπουλος 9, Σάρμα 4, Γκαντ 18 (4), Τζόουνς 6, Ρόμπινσον 7 (1), Τσαϊρέλης 2, Πουλιανίτης, Χατζηνικόλας, Βησσαρίου ΑΡΗΣ (Σπανούλης): Μήτρου-Λονγκ 12 (1), Ρόμπινσον-Ερλ 17 (1), Ντιμιτρίεβιτς 25 (6), Κ. Αντετοκούνμπο 9, Μοκόκα 1, Τολιόπουλος 5 (1), Χατζηλάμπρου, Πουλιανίτης, Γιόβιτς 3 (1), Λιντέλ 14, Θ. Αντετοκούνμπο, Μπιρτς 2 www.ertnews.gr

items.descriptionOriginal: As temperatures rise across the globe, scientists have identified a specialized lipid barrier that protects developing fruit flies from dehydration. This finding may help explain insects’ ability to adapt to changing temperatures. Fruit flies, or Drosophila, begin life as larvae that feed and burrow in decomposing fruit. Before becoming adults, they move to drier environments and enter the pupal stage, during which they undergo metamorphosis. According to the team at the Francis Crick Institute, adult fruit flies have a hydrophobic lipid coating made of long hydrocarbon molecules that blocks water loss. Before this, researchers did not know how pupae protected themselves against dehydration. To investigate this protective mechanism, the team adapted analytical methods used in the petroleum industry and combined them with molecular imaging techniques. Secret to hydration The researchers found no detectable hydrocarbons on the outer body of the pupae, called the cuticle. Instead, the protective barrier was lined on the inner side of the cuticle and contained hyper-long hydrocarbons, much longer than those typically found on mature adult flies . The study also found that specialized cells in the larva, called oenocytes, produce these hydrocarbons before metamorphosis. The molecules are stored in the larval fat body until they are needed during the transition to the pupal stage. Co-first author and principal laboratory research scientist at the institute, Clare Newell said that the immobile pupal stage is especially vulnerable because it cannot move to a cooler or less dry environment. “It’s fascinating that the larva prepares for this challenge before metamorphosis, building a resource of hyper-long hydrocarbons. Embracing techniques normally used outside biology helped us to reveal one of the many hidden secrets of metamorphosis,” she added. In the study, they discovered “a key enzyme that ensures the development of a specific lipid barrier in the pupa that protects it from water loss in hot and arid conditions.” The researchers noted that Drosophila can survive only within certain environmental limits, and their research on this enzyme has helped define those boundaries. According to the study, longer hydrocarbons were associated with greater dehydration resistance. Shorter hydrocarbons were more volatile and functioned as airborne chemical signals. The researchers examined six fruit fly species and found that five generally transitioned toward shorter hydrocarbons during adult maturation. However, the desert species Drosophila mojavensis retained hyper-long hydrocarbons even as an adult. The study’s authors suggested that maintaining these longer molecules may reflect the importance of dehydration resistance in arid environments, possibly helping their survival in extreme conditions. Climate change impacts insects The researchers concluded that the lipid barrier protecting Drosophila melanogaster during metamorphosis cannot prevent lethal dehydration when high temperatures and low humidity occur together. That concerns how climate change might affect these insects . According to the study, “These humidity and temperature values are found in many areas of our planet, so given the pace of climate change, D. melanogaster and some other species may struggle to adapt rapidly enough to survive within some or all of their current geographical ranges.” Alex Gould, group leader of the Physiology and Metabolism Laboratory at the Crick and senior author, emphasized the importance of understanding insect survival under changing environmental conditions. “Insects are vital to life on Earth, pollinating three-quarters of global food crop species. With the backdrop of human-induced climate change, it’s important to understand the resilience of insects to increases in aridity and temperature. We hope that this work in Drosophila will inspire similar research in other insect species, including those that play an important role in our food chains,” Gould added. The findings were recently published in Science Advances .

items.descriptionOriginal: Τα φρούτα θεωρούνται ισχυρός σύμμαχος της υγείας. Ωστόσο, από ότι φαίνεται δεν είναι όλα εξίσου ωφέλιμα για το πεπτικό μας σύστημα . Ένας γαστρεντερολόγος από το Harvard κατέταξε 10 από τα πιο συνηθισμένα φρούτα με βάση το πώς επηρεάζουν το έντερο , αποκαλύπτοντας ποιο αποφεύγει πάντοτε και ποια βρίσκονται στην κορυφή της λίστας του. Σύμφωνα με τον Δρ. Saurabh Sethi , οι (υπερ)ώριμες μπανάνες συγκαταλέγονται στις χειρότερες επιλογές . Λόγω της υψηλής περιεκτικότητάς τους σε σάκχαρα, ανεβάζουν απότομα το σάκχαρο και δεν τροφοδοτούν σωστά τα ωφέλιμα βακτήρια του εντέρου. Όπως εξηγεί, όσο ωριμάζει μια μπανάνα, τόσο χάνει φυτικές ίνες και ανθεκτικό άμυλο -ουσίες που λειτουργούν ως πρεβιοτικά. Αντίθετα, οι ελαφρώς άγουρες μπανάνες περιέχουν περισσότερες φυτικές ίνες και συμβάλλουν στην πρόληψη καρδιαγγειακών παθήσεων, διαβήτη τύπου 2 και καρκίνου του παχέος εντέρου . Τα φρούτα που βοηθούν την πέψη Στην πρώτη θέση της λίστας του βρίσκονται τα μύρτιλα , τα οποία είναι πλούσια σε αντιοξειδωτικά και θωρακίζουν τον οργανισμό από χρόνιες ασθένειες. Ακολουθεί το ρόδι , το οποίο περιέχει πολυφαινόλες που μειώνουν τη φλεγμονή, έναν από τους βασικούς παράγοντες κινδύνου για καρδιοπάθειες. Επίσης, τα ακτινίδια ξεχωρίζουν χάρη στις διαλυτές φυτικές τους ίνες, που διευκολύνουν τη δυσκοιλιότητα και συμβάλλουν σε πιο τακτικές κενώσεις. Σταφύλια, πορτοκάλια και άλλες (μέσες) επιλογές Στη μέση της κατάταξης βρίσκονται τα μήλα , τα αχλάδια και τα πεπόνια , ενώ πιο χαμηλά συναντώνται τα σταφύλια και τα πορτοκάλια . Παρότι τα σταφύλια περιέχουν βιταμίνη C και κάλιο , θεωρούνται φτωχότερα σε συνολική θρεπτική αξία σε σχέση με άλλα φρούτα. Στο ίδιο μήκος κύματος, τα πορτοκάλια, αν και είναι πλούσια σε βιταμίνη C, φολικό οξύ και αντιοξειδωτικά, μελέτη έχει συνδέσει την υπερβολική κατανάλωση εσπεριδοειδών με αυξημένο κίνδυνο καρκίνου του δέρματος . Οι ειδικοί αποδίδουν το φαινόμενο στις φωτοευαισθητοποιές ιδιότητες των φρούτων, αν και απαιτείται περαιτέρω έρευνα. Ωστόσο, η βιταμίνη C παραμένει απαραίτητη για το (υγιές) δέρμα, τα αιμοφόρα αγγεία, τα οστά και τους χόνδρους. Αξίζει να σημειωθεί ότι δεν αποθηκεύεται στο σώμα και, επομένως, πρέπει να λαμβάνεται καθημερινά από τη διατροφή ή, εφόσον χρειάζεται, από συμπληρώματα. Δείτε αυτή τη δημοσίευση στο Instagram. Η δημοσίευση κοινοποιήθηκε από το χρήστη Saurabh Sethi MD MPH | Gastroenterologist (@doctor.sethi) Η κατάταξη με μια ματιά Μύρτιλα Ρόδι Ακτινίδια Μήλα Αχλάδια Ελαφρώς άγουρες μπανάνες Πεπόνια Πορτοκάλια Σταφύλια Υπερώριμες μπανάνες. Διαβάστε επίσης Τι συμβαίνει στο σώμα μας όταν δεν καταναλώνουμε αρκετές φυτικές ίνες Το καλοκαιρινό φρούτο που προστατεύει καρδιά, μαλλιά και επιδερμίδα Φυτικές ίνες: Η νέα εμμονή του TikTok μετά την πρωτεΐνη – Οι ειδικοί εξηγούν αν αξίζει

items.descriptionOriginal: An electrical domain with an area smaller than 1 nm² could offer a clue to fitting more memory onto a chip. Researchers working with Washington University in St. Louis observed domains that small in zirconia, a material chemically similar to an insulator already used in silicon transistors. In a separate study, they identified a way to switch the electrical structure of thin films made from that insulator, known as hafnia. The studies involved Washington University materials scientist Rohan Mishra and collaborators at the University of Nebraska–Lincoln, Georgia Tech and South Korea’s UNIST, among others. The teams combined atomic-scale simulations with electron microscopy and experiments to see how changes in the two materials could help meet growing demand for denser data storage as AI use expands. Turning a chip insulator into a memory candidate Hafnia forms a thin insulating layer in silicon transistors. Its appeal for memory lies in a property called ferroelectricity. An electric field can flip the direction of a ferroelectric material’s polarization, and the material holds that orientation after the field is removed. Those two orientations could encode digital information. Most ferroelectric materials lose that behavior when thinned below about 10 nanometers. Earlier work by researchers in Germany showed that hafnia behaves differently. It can become ferroelectric in extremely thin films, even though the bulk material typically lacks that property. To understand what drives the change, Mishra’s team worked with researchers at the University of Nebraska–Lincoln to grow single-crystal films of lanthanum-doped hafnia. Guodong Ren, then a doctoral student in Mishra’s group, used electron microscopy to resolve individual columns of atoms. The crystal structure his team identified matched its computational predictions. Switching hafnia with an electric field The findings suggest engineers could grow hafnia in a stable antiferroelectric structure and then use an electric field to switch it during operation. In an antiferroelectric structure, neighboring polarizations point in opposite directions. The applied field can drive the film into a different electrical state. “Instead of fighting nature, we can grow high-quality antiferroelectric films and we can then switch them during operation,” Mishra said. The same materials could also have a role in energy storage. Mishra said antiferroelectrics can store large amounts of energy, making them candidates for high-energy-density capacitors. Oxygen helps stabilize tiny zirconia domains In the zirconia study, researchers found regions smaller than one square nanometer in which electrical polarization pointed in a consistent direction. Extra oxygen atoms helped balance the charge where neighboring regions met. The team’s calculations predicted that these boundaries, known as domain walls, could conduct electricity and move when a voltage was applied. If engineers can control that movement, the walls could eventually serve as components in memory devices. The two studies point to different ways of controlling electrical behavior at the scale of individual atoms. Hafnia offers a route through a switchable crystal structure, while zirconia raises the possibility of using the boundaries themselves. Hafnia’s existing role in silicon transistors gives engineers a familiar material to work with as they explore how to turn those findings into memory. The studies were published in Advanced Materials and Science journals.

items.title: Μετά από μια αποτυχημένη καλλιέργεια, ο 57χρονος αγρότης καλλιέργησε φράουλες χωρίς χώμα και έκανε 44 Lakh Rs σε πωλήσεις
items.titleOriginal: After a Failed Crop, 57-YO Farmer Grew Strawberries Without Soil & Made Rs 44 Lakh in Sales
items.description: «Η καλλιέργεια σταματά εντελώς κατά τους καλοκαιρινούς και τους μουσώνες μήνες, επειδή η καλλιέργεια φράουλας σε ανοιχτό χωράφι δεν μπορεί να επιβιώσει αυτού του είδους τη ζέστη και τις βροχοπτώσεις». Για γενιές, αυτός ήταν ο κύκλος της καλλιέργειας φράουλας στο Mahabaleshwar. Όταν ο καιρός ζεστάνει και φτάνουν οι βροχές, η εποχή της φράουλας φτάνει στο τέλος της. Αλλά ο 57χρονος Ketan Sodha…
items.descriptionOriginal: "Cultivation stops completely through summer and monsoon months, because open-field strawberry growing cannot survive that kind of heat and rainfall." For generations, this has been the cycle of strawberry farming in Mahabaleshwar . When the weather turns warm, and the rains arrive, the strawberry season comes to an end. But 57-year-old Ketan Sodha, who had never farmed before 2016, wanted to see whether the season could last longer. A fourth-generation Mumbaikar from a business family with no farming background, Ketan completed his BCom from K C College under Mumbai University. He spent years connecting agricultural landowners with buyers across Maharashtra. Then, in 2016, demonetisation changed the business he knew. "What was available was Rs 25,000 an acre. In two years, it went up to Rs 3 lakh," he recalls of the agricultural land boom he had witnessed. But when demonetisation hit, that business slowed dramatically. "I had to start something new, so I decided to switch over to Mahabaleshwar for strawberries," he tells The Better India. Today, his venture, Berry Fresh Agrotech LLP, has a soilless polyhouse in Mahabaleshwar with the capacity to grow 19,500 strawberry plants. The farm has reportedly produced around 8,000 kg of fruit and generated Rs 44 lakh in sales. But getting here began with 5,000 plants, a failed crop, and a man from Mumbai learning to farm for the first time. How a first-time farmer learnt from his mistakes His work dealing in agricultural land took him across Maharashtra, usually within 200 km of Mumbai. One of the routes he travelled frequently was towards Goa, passing through Poladpur and the foothills of Mahabaleshwar. 57-year-old Ketan Sodha, who had never farmed before 2016, wanted to see whether the season could last longer. For someone used to Mumbai, Mahabaleshwar felt like another world. "I was born and raised in Mumbai, so coming here was a great delight for me. The city is hot, humid and congested, whereas spending a night in the cool hills around Poladpur felt like a completely different world," he admits. He first became interested in strawberries around 2012-13. After his land business slowed in 2016, he bought 5,000 plants from a local farmer and tried growing them himself. "The first year actually was a disaster," he says. But he did not walk away. In 2017, he increased the number of plants to 10,000. This time, the results were different. He began producing more fruit than many conventional growers around him who had been cultivating strawberries for decades. "My name began spreading in the area, and people started saying, 'This guy seems to know something we don't,'" he recalls. Some farmers began approaching him for partnerships, and he accepted a few of those opportunities. By 2019, he had entered into a partnership and started cultivating strawberries across nine acres. By the 2020-21 season, his operations had expanded to almost 40 acres across three sites. He was also working with imported planting material and developing his own nurseries. But even as his farming operations grew, the weather remained a challenge he could not control. The rain spoilt his hard work Mahabaleshwar may be known for its strawberries, but the crop is traditionally grown in open fields. That leaves the plants exposed to everything the weather brings. Ketan repeatedly saw the same problem during the years he spent growing the fruit conventionally. Unseasonal rain would arrive around November and early December, just when the crop was reaching its peak. The rain could set the crop back by 15 to 20 days. "You need to recover the crop, take care of it, spray some fungicides, because the unexpected rain creates a lot of nuisance," he says. There was another limitation too. Once summer and the monsoon arrived, conventional strawberry cultivation stopped. He began wondering whether changing the environment in which strawberries grew could help him extend the season, rather than leaving his harvest at the mercy of the weather. 4 countries, countless lessons and one Indian challenge In 2021-22, he travelled to Italy, Spain, Egypt and Turkey. He met nursery owners and hydroponic growers and spoke to consultants from several countries, including Israel, the UK, New Zealand, Australia and the US. He came back with plenty of information. But he also came back with an important realisation. A system that worked perfectly in another country could not blindly be copied in India. "My country's challenges are very different from what they are working on in their own native area," he says. He began developing a model suited to the conditions in Mahabaleshwar. Berry Fresh Agrotech LLP was incorporated on 14 October 2022. He had already been cultivating strawberries conventionally with local farmers. But the company's soilless plantation began in November 2024. Before the first plants went into the new system, he spent around three-and-a-half months searching for suitable land , despite having worked in the region for years. He eventually leased two acres. On this land, he built a 1,500-square-metre polyhouse designed to accommodate 19,500 strawberry plants. And this time, there would be no soil. A strawberry farm without soil Inside his polyhouse, the plants grow in cocopeat, a growing medium made from coconut husk. Traditional strawberry fields use the same soil year after year, increasing the risk of soil-borne diseases. Growing the plants in cocopeat helps reduce this risk. The plants are grown under a retractable roof in an openable polyhouse. A misting system helps manage the growing environment. The farm is also located at an altitude of around 1,400 metres. Even when temperatures rise suddenly in the plains, Mahabaleshwar's elevation gives the plants a natural advantage. Then comes water. Through an automated fertigation system, which delivers water and nutrients together, each plant receives approximately 75 ml of nutrient solution over 24 hours. His farm also harvests rainwater and stores it for use. Before entering the growing system, the water is treated with ozone. Today, his venture, Berry Fresh Agrotech LLP, has a soilless polyhouse in Mahabaleshwar with the capacity to grow 19,500 strawberry plants. This allows him to manage the water supply while reducing dependence on external sources or groundwater. "The plant is never stressed by too much or too little water," he explains. Together, the soilless growing medium, measured nutrients, protected environment and milder temperatures help Ketan keep his strawberry plants growing during periods when conventional cultivation stops. "The real innovation here is not one single trick, but removing every variable, one by one, that used to force conventional growers to stop," he explains. There are parts of the process he does not disclose. Those, he says, are the lessons he has gathered through years of experimentation and practical work. And much of that learning came from problems he had to solve himself. When everything had to be rebuilt He had initially expected specialised vendors to provide much of the technology required for the farm. Instead, several systems needed to be fixed and recalibrated. The polyhouse took more than six months to complete. The automation and irrigation systems also required considerable attention. Even finding suitable hydroponic-grade fertilisers proved difficult. Eventually, he and his team began inspecting, repairing and adjusting the pipes, valves, sensors, controllers and irrigation lines themselves. "We started this journey to grow strawberries, not to become experts in polyhouse construction, irrigation, automation and fertigation," he says. "When a problem arises, we don't have to wait for someone to fly in or send a technician," he says. "We understand our systems because we have rebuilt many of them ourselves." The entire setup required an investment in the seven-figure range, although he does not want to disclose the exact amount. He viewed the first facility as a place to experiment and learn, rather than recover the investment immediately. Testing 19 varieties for Indian conditions Ketan is among only around 12 to 15 growers in India involved in importing strawberry planting material. Berry Fresh is currently conducting trials involving 19 strawberry varieties from countries including Florida, Spain, Italy, Uruguay and Japan. This season, the farm has also added a variety from the Netherlands. Different varieties respond differently to climate and disease, and can vary in yield, taste and fruit quality. A variety that performs well abroad may struggle in Indian conditions. Through these trials, Ketan wants to identify which varieties grow best here and eventually make better planting material accessible to other farmers. He is also exploring the possibility of securing exclusive rights to some foreign genetics for India as he works towards expanding the business. The plants are grown under a retractable roof in an openable polyhouse. From a failed crop to Rs 44 lakh in sales The current facility has an installed capacity of 19,500 plants and operates at around 90 percent capacity. For the period from January 2024 to December 2025, Ketan reports an average harvest of 408 grams per plant, with production of approximately 3.2 kg per square metre. Across the production figures shared by Berry Fresh, the venture has reportedly harvested approximately 8,000 kg of strawberries and generated around Rs 44 lakh in revenue through business-to-business (B2B) and direct-to-consumer (B2C) sales. The strawberries are sold at an approximate price of Rs 400 to Rs 600 per kg, depending on the customer and order. Around 60 percent of sales are B2C, while 40 percent are B2B. Its customers are spread across Mumbai, Mahabaleshwar, Delhi, Bhopal, Ahmedabad, Indore, Udupi and Goa. There is no comprehensive digital marketing operation behind those sales. Ketan admits he has no social media presence. Instead, his customers have largely found him through word of mouth. And many of them have stayed. 'Do not pay if you do not like it' Prashant Tatia (54), from Bhopal, runs a premium fruit and dry-fruit shop. He has known Ketan since 2021 and started purchasing strawberries from Berry Fresh in January 2025. Berry Fresh Agrotech LLP was incorporated on 14 October 2022. "The strawberries produced by the farm are distinctly different from conventionally grown open-field varieties," says Prashant. "They stand out for their vibrant colour, natural shine, uniform shape, exceptional taste, higher sweetness, longer shelf life, and outstandingly rich aroma." For Prashant, the consistency matters just as much as the taste. He says the quality remains consistent even during the off-season. "What sets Berry Fresh apart is its year-round availability and consistently high quality," he says. Luvjeet Singh, an imported fruit dealer from Vashi, Mumbai, began purchasing from the venture in November 2025. Ketan had contacted him the previous month. "He simply quoted, 'Do not pay if you do not like it,'" Luvjeet recalls. "I was surprised by his confidence, hence thought of trying. It was worth his claim." He says the berries differ in their colour, shine, shape, sweetness, aroma and shelf life, and believes his customers are willing to pay for better-quality produce. In Ahmedabad, 25-year-old Apurva Shelat came across the business through a common friend. She began buying the strawberries in November 2025. "After talking to the founder, I developed trust, so I decided to try his strawberries," she says. "I found that the quality was much better, and my community also liked them very much." She has also visited the farm. For someone who had never seen this kind of strawberry cultivation before, the experience changed the way she looked at farming. "I was impressed by how clean, well-organised and professionally managed the farm was. Seeing the hydroponic system for the first time also changed my understanding of modern farming," she says. His next bet: 2 lakh plants across 5 acres For now, Berry Fresh operates only in Mahabaleshwar. But the founder is already thinking beyond the 19,500 plants. He is currently at the investor-discussion stage for a proposed five-acre facility with a minimum capacity of around 200,000 plants. He wants to build the next farm using everything he has learnt from the first, with the hope of eventually replicating the model in other parts of India where the climate is suitable. The opportunity, in his view, is to grow strawberries during months when fewer farmers can supply them, and when the fruit can fetch better prices. "If we can extend the production window at both ends, early fruit before the regular season starts, and no-season fruit after everyone else has stopped, both of those windows fetch the highest value in the market," he says. It is a different life from the one he knew in Mumbai. Ketan had no family farming background, and his first attempt at growing strawberries failed. Today, he spends his days learning how to help thousands of plants thrive in the hills he has come to love. On this land, he built a 1,500-square-metre polyhouse designed to accommodate 19,500 strawberry plants. "Every morning, birds wake me up before any alarm does," he says. "The air here is crisp, the spring water is clean, and there is a kind of peace around this farm that you cannot buy in Mumbai." For Ketan, the next challenge is taking what he has learnt from this first polyhouse to a much larger farm, while continuing to explore how far Mahabaleshwar's strawberry season can stretch. All pictures courtesy Ketan Sodha.

items.description: Αυτή η ιστορία είναι μέρος του "India Invented This?" — Η εβδομαδιαία σειρά trivia του The Better India που αποκαλύπτει τα μυαλά, τις ιδέες και τις καινοτομίες των Ινδών πίσω από εφευρέσεις που έχουν διαμορφώσει τον τρόπο που ζούμε. Από έξυπνες λύσεις που δημιουργήθηκαν από επιστήμονες και μηχανικούς έως τεχνολογίες που αναπτύχθηκαν ως απάντηση σε μερικές από τις μεγαλύτερες προκλήσεις της Ινδίας, κάθε ιστορία πάει μακρυά…
items.descriptionOriginal: This story is part of "India Invented This?" — The Better India's weekly trivia series that uncovers the Indian minds, ideas and innovations behind inventions that have shaped the way we live. From ingenious solutions created by scientists and engineers to technologies developed in response to some of India's biggest challenges, each story goes beyond the invention to explore the problem it solved, the impact it created and why it still matters today. There is something special about the moment a child lights their first sparkler. The excitement of holding it, the little circles they draw in the air, and the delight of watching it fade into tiny glowing embers are memories that often stay with us long after childhood. For generations, firecrackers have been part of how many Indian families celebrate Diwali. But what if the thrill of watching something burst into the sky did not have to come with clouds of smoke, lingering gunpowder smells and piles of burnt debris? That was the question Dr Samrat Ghosh, a chemical scientist at the Indian Institute of Science Education and Research (IISER), Mohali, decided to explore. His answer? A firecracker that uses an entirely different approach to create the familiar excitement of fireworks, without the smoke and particulate emissions associated with conventional crackers. And the interesting part is that his innovation began with something most people would simply throw away: an empty plastic bottle. From waste bottles to a new kind of firecracker In October 2017, following concerns about firecracker pollution and a Supreme Court order temporarily restricting their use in the NCR, then Union Environment Minister Dr Harsh Vardhan called upon scientists to develop safer alternatives , including electronic firecrackers. Dr Samrat took up the challenge. A discarded plastic bottle became the starting point for an innovation that rethinks conventional fireworks. Photograph: ( The Indian Express ) An assistant professor in IISER Mohali's Department of Chemical Sciences, he drew upon his expertise in combustion chemistry to develop what became known as the IISER-M pollution-free firecracker. The first prototype was built using recycled plastic bottles and a specially developed combustible formulation. Instead of the conventional arrangement of chemicals packed into a paper casing, his device worked through a small launcher mechanism. Here's how it worked: When triggered by a spark , the combustible material ignited and generated pressure, pushing the bottle upwards like a rocket. The launch produced a loud bang, recreating some of the excitement associated with traditional fireworks. But the real innovation lay in what happened around it. No smoke, no leftover debris, and even a fragrance! Unlike conventional firecrackers, Ghosh's formulation was designed to produce no visible smoke or particulate matter. The device also left no conventional firecracker debris behind. Another unusual feature was that the sound level could be adjusted, allowing users to customise how loud the explosion was. Depending on the ingredients used in the combustible formulation , the device could even release a fragrance into the air. The idea was to replace the familiar smell of gunpowder with something more pleasant. Imagine finishing Diwali celebrations with the scent of lavender rather than burnt chemicals! The IISER-M firecracker uses a launcher mechanism to recreate the excitement of traditional rockets. Photograph: ( ANI News ) His team developed both aerial and non-aerial prototypes. The device was also designed to be reusable, with the bottle being launched rather than destroyed in the process. The next experiment involved something unexpected A year after developing the prototype, Ghosh and his team began exploring ways to make the formulation more affordable. Their next experiment involved distilled cow urine. In 2019, the team had developed a cheaper version of its green firecracker using this ingredient. According to Ghosh, incorporating distilled cow urine reduced the cost of the formulation by 50%, without changing its performance in terms of sound, light and flight. The team also maintained that its organic formulation produced no particulate-matter emissions. An emission study was being conducted at IISER to analyse the gases released during combustion. The experiment was also driven by a practical consideration: making the technology affordable enough to explore wider adoption. A different way to look at celebration For Ghosh, the idea was never simply to make another firecracker. It was to rethink how fireworks could work while addressing some of the problems associated with conventional ones. His innovation also had potential applications beyond Diwali. The device could potentially be used to drive animals away from agricultural fields or help clear airport runways. The technology was still under development according to the reports in 2018, and its commercialisation and wider adoption were not established. The innovation was still awaiting patents at the time of the reports, and its journey towards wider commercial use remained a work in progress. The innovation explores alternatives to conventional crackers, including adjustable sound levels and fragrance-releasing formulations. Photograph: ( Hindustan Times ) But perhaps that is what makes the experiment interesting. It shows how even the most familiar traditions can leave room for new ideas. A discarded plastic bottle, a scientist's curiosity and a desire to reduce pollution came together to challenge the way we think about firecrackers. And who knows? With further research and development, innovations like Ghosh's could one day help make the excitement of Diwali a little kinder to the air we all share. Sources: 'This Diwali go for this pollution-free firecracker' by Business Standard, Published on 29 April 2018. 'Mohali scientist makes fireworks with cow urine' by Shimona Kanwar for The Times of India, Published on 22 April 2019.

items.description: Ένας Πολωνός μοναχός ξεκινούσε κάθε μέρα με επτά τόξα -- μια χειρονομία συγγνώμης προς έναν πατέρα που δεν μπορούσε να αντιμετωπίσει. Η ιστορία του Bhikshu Jin Wei δεν είναι ένα τακτοποιημένο τόξο πνευματικής προόδου. Είναι μια ειλικρινής περιγραφή του πώς η πείνα για μεταμόρφωση μπορεί να γίνει η δική της παγίδα και η ήπια διαδικασία συντονισμού με κάθε στιγμή. Η στροφή ήρθε αθόρυβα, μέσα από ένα μόνο χτύπημα…
items.descriptionOriginal: A Polish monk began each day with seven bows -- a gesture of apology toward a father he couldn't face. Bhikshu Jin Wei's story is not a tidy arc of spiritual progress; it's an honest account of how the hunger for transformation can become its own trap, and the gentle process of attuning to each moment. The turning came quietly, through a single word: a Thai Forest monk suggested a one-word loving-kindness mantra, and Jin Wei sat in the meditation hall asking himself what his word was. Immediately, it came: "safe". What followed was the discovery that the compassion he had been excavating through discipline had been waiting in his body all along -- "our body remembers our trauma," he reflects, "but the body also keeps the love." While on a trip back to Poland earlier this year, he experienced profound, full-circle moments along a softening journey: giving a talk at his own university and sitting down to a vegetarian lunch lovingly offered by his meat-eating family. The monastery, he suggests, is not only a physical place but a quality of listening, available to anyone willing to stop and ask what word is waiting to open their heart.

items.descriptionOriginal: The first sign that winter has arrived in many North Indian kitchens is not the chill in the morning air, but the sight of a heap of red carrots at the vegetable market. For a few months, the deep-red carrot takes centre stage in markets across Delhi and other parts of North India, where shoppers who buy orange carrots through much of the year will seek out this seasonal variety. But the red carrot's place in the winter kitchen is tied to more than nostalgia. Its cultivation depends on growing conditions, including temperature, raising questions about what warmer winters could mean for a crop so closely associated with the season. Why red carrots rule the winter kitchen Red carrots, commonly known as lal gajar, are prized for their deep colour, sweetness and juiciness. Their arrival makes a difference to dishes in which the vegetable is the main ingredient, rather than simply one component of a meal. In gajar ka halwa, grated red carrots cook down with milk and ghee to produce the dessert's characteristic colour and flavour. Kanji draws on a different tradition: carrot sticks ferment in water seasoned with mustard seeds, salt and spices, producing a sharp, tangy drink. Red carrots are also used in winter salads, cooked vegetable dishes and pickles. Its arrival signals the season for halwa made in large batches, jars of kanji left to ferment and pickles prepared for later consumption. Photograph: (Bliss of Cooking; Your Everyday Cook) The seasonal preference for red carrots is therefore not simply a switch from one colour to another. It is also about the taste, texture and culinary traditions associated with the red variety. There is a scientific reason to look beyond colour. In a study published in 2016 in the Indian Journal of Agricultural Sciences, researchers Swati Saha, Pritam Kalia, Amish Kumar Sureja and S Sarkar at the ICAR–Indian Agricultural Research Institute in New Delhi examined 38 tropical carrot lines over four consecutive years, from 2009 to 2012. They compared characteristics including root weight, colour and nutritional composition. The researchers found considerable differences in the amount of carotenoids and other pigments present in the carrots. One red line, IPC-11 red, contained 9.99 milligrams of total carotenoids per 100 grams. The study also found that some carrot lines performed well under high-temperature conditions , making them potential candidates for future breeding. A crop shaped by temperature Carrots are generally associated with cool-season cultivation, although tropical varieties have been developed to grow under warmer conditions. Temperature influences root development, yield and quality, making it an important factor in determining how successfully a variety performs. Saha and her colleagues put it simply: 'Temperature influences growth, yield and quality of carrots in many different ways.' Their research was not a study of climate change in farmers' fields. Instead, it explored whether particular carrot lines could withstand heat while retaining desirable characteristics. The researchers noted that 'some inbreds performed well under extreme high temperature without affecting any quality attributes'. Such lines, they suggested, could be selected for further breeding. Temperature influences root development, yield and quality, making it an important factor in determining how successfully a variety performs. Photograph: (Adobe Stock) India's agricultural research system also maintains red varieties suited to local growing conditions. In a 2020 article in the ICAR journal Indian Horticulture, researchers described Pusa Kesar as a variety with deep-red roots and a small, deep-red core. They also documented Pusa Rudhira, developed by ICAR-IARI in New Delhi, as a tropical variety with dark-red roots that matures around 85–90 days after sowing and is suitable for cultivation in the National Capital Region. These varieties show how researchers have worked to develop carrots suited to India's agricultural conditions. But they also raise a question: how might the conditions in which red carrots are grown change as temperatures rise? What warming winters could mean The 2016 study offers a useful starting point for understanding the risks. In discussing earlier research on carrot cultivation, Saha and her colleagues noted that temperatures above 25 C could result in unmarketable roots and lower yields. They also cited research indicating that temperatures below 10 C or above 30 C could produce lighter-coloured roots. These findings point to a potential concern for growers: that heat can affect not just how much a crop produces, but also the appearance and quality of its roots. For red carrots, whose colour is central to their appeal, that factor is important. However, these temperature findings should not be treated as proof that climate change is already reducing red carrot production in North India. The effects depend on the variety, the timing of sowing, soil conditions, irrigation and temperatures at different stages of growth. Preserving a seasonal flavour The red carrot's winter popularity connects agriculture to everyday food traditions. Its arrival signals the season for halwa made in large batches, jars of kanji left to ferment and pickles prepared for later consumption. The future of this seasonal crop will depend partly on how effectively farmers and breeders respond to changing growing conditions. Until then, the seasonal rush for red carrots remains both a culinary tradition and a reason to pay closer attention to the crops that connect India's winter kitchens to its changing climate. Sources: 'Climate change and vegetable crops cultivation: A review' : By The Indian Journal of Agricultural Sciences, Published on 27 April 2018 'Response of carrot (Daucus carota L.) cultivars to different sowing dates on growth and yield' : By P Madhavi Latha, P Syam Sundar Reddy, Ramanjaneya Reddy, V Sudha Vani, Published on 30 December 2015 'Breeding tropical carrots (Daucus carota) for enhanced nutrition and high temperature stress' : By ICAR-Indian Agricultural Research Institute, Pusa, Published on 11 July 2016

items.title: «Είχαν χάσει την ελπίδα τους»: Πώς μια ομάδα που υποστηρίζεται από IIT πήρε τρόφιμα και φάρμακα σε 1000+ άτομα στο Πλημμυρισμένο Assam
items.titleOriginal: ‘They Had Lost Hope’: How an IIT-Backed Team Took Food & Meds to 1000+ People in Flood-Hit Assam
items.description: «Άνθρωποι, ζώα, γεωργικά χωράφια – τα πάντα έχουν πληγεί σοβαρά», λέει ο Dakshina, κάτοικος της Nazira στο Assam που είδε τις πλημμύρες. «Δεν υπήρχαν δρόμοι, ούτε γέφυρες, ούτε προσβάσιμες διαδρομές γιατί τα πάντα ήταν βυθισμένα στο νερό». Όταν τα νερά της πλημμύρας καταπίνουν δρόμους, καλύπτουν γέφυρες και περιβάλλουν ολόκληρους οικισμούς, ζητώντας βοήθεια στο p…
items.descriptionOriginal: "People, animals, agricultural fields – everything has been severely affected," says Dakshina, a resident of Nazira in Assam who witnessed the floods. "There were no roads, no bridges, and no accessible routes because everything was submerged in water." When floodwaters swallow roads, cover bridges and surround entire settlements, getting help to people becomes a race against time. In Assam, where communities face recurring floods, even getting essential supplies to stranded residents can become a challenge. During the recent floods in Upper Assam, parts of Sivasagar and other affected districts faced precisely this problem. Water had cut off communities from the road network, and in some places, even boats struggled to reach people because the water was too shallow. For residents, the uncertainty was frightening. People had to find safer ground while trying to save their livestock and livelihoods. Some were stranded in places where rescue teams could not easily reach them. In this situation, Drones Tech Lab, a deep-tech company incubated at the Indian Institute of Technology (IIT) Guwahati, deployed payload-carrying drones to deliver food, water, medicines and other essentials across three districts in Assam. The operation reached more than 1,000 people in locations where even conventional relief efforts faced access constraints. The drones also helped survey affected areas and identify stranded residents, giving relief and rescue teams a clearer picture of where assistance was needed. For Dakshina, the intervention revealed a side of drone technology she had never seen before. When floodwaters cut off roads and bridges, drones helped deliver essential supplies to communities stranded in Assam. "Usually, we know drones as something used for taking videos at parties, weddings, or similar events," she says. "But this time, we saw for the first time how drones can actually help people during a disaster." Behind this intervention was technology that had taken years to develop , test and adapt for India's challenging terrain. 'We wanted India to build its own drones' Founded in 2016 by Ritesh Kanu, Biswajit Dey and Debajit Deka, Drones Tech Lab began with a vision to develop indigenous drone capabilities in a country that relied heavily on foreign technology. At the time, India's drone ecosystem was still taking shape. Awareness of its applications beyond photography was limited, access to funding was difficult, and building hardware-intensive technology came with significant challenges. Kanu says the founders wanted to address the dependence on imported systems and build technology suited to India's operational needs. "India has been a consumer of drone technology right from the start," he says. "We had a belief and a vision that we should be building in assets." For the team, indigenous technology did not mean manufacturing every component locally from day one. It meant developing intellectual property, designing system architecture, integrating software and engineering drones for specific missions. Their early work was influenced by the challenges faced by defence personnel operating in difficult environments. The founders saw how technology could help reduce risks to human life, particularly when information about a location or threat was difficult to obtain. Through its association with IIT Guwahati, the company developed unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), flight systems, software and specialised payload mechanisms. Developed at IIT Guwahati, Drones Tech Lab's heavy-payload drone can carry up to 30 kg, with applications ranging from disaster response to healthcare logistics. One of its developments was a heavy-payload drone with an indigenous carbon-fibre frame capable of carrying up to 30 kg. The company has since worked across disaster response, defence, healthcare logistics, mapping, conservation and infrastructure. Kanu compares a drone's carbon-fibre frame to a car's chassis: it holds the different components together. Its propulsion system, which includes motors and electronic speed controllers, provides the force needed to lift and move the drone. The real capability, however, lies in how these components work together. By modifying software, propulsion systems and payload-release mechanisms, the team can adapt a drone to the requirements of a particular mission. During a flood , that could mean carrying essential supplies to a settlement cut off by water. A drone can take help to floot-hit villages The first challenge during a flood is understanding what is happening on the ground. Which settlements are cut off? Where are people stranded? Which areas need supplies most urgently? And how can rescue teams approach them safely? Drones can survey affected areas from above, helping teams map isolated pockets and prioritise their response. Once a delivery point is identified, its coordinates can be entered into the flight plan. The drone then carries the supplies to the designated location, where the package is released for people on the ground to collect. During the Assam operation , Drones Tech Lab used drones with a payload capacity of around 5 kg per flight. They travelled approximately 5 km on missions that took about 25 minutes. The smaller payload was a deliberate choice based on the conditions. "We have drones that can carry more than 50 kilos also," says Kanu. "But the situation demanded a drone with a payload capacity of around 5 kg to make the operation more effective." The process involved much more than flying an aircraft. The team mapped affected locations, coordinated with government officials, prepared supply packets and identified suitable delivery points. Local authorities helped the team reach launch locations and coordinate its work with relief efforts. During the Assam floods, the team used drones carrying around 5 kg per flight, covering approximately 5 km in 25 minutes. Together, these steps helped the team plan where supplies needed to go and how to get them there. Drones also helped responders understand the condition of stranded residents. Dakshina recalls how aerial surveys identified people on rooftops or trapped alongside their livestock, while providing information about water levels and possible routes for rescue teams. When immediate physical rescue was not possible, aerial assessments helped teams determine whether people had food and water and needed urgent assistance. Every disaster taught them something new The company had already deployed its technology during the 2022 Assam floods and following Cyclone Amphan in West Bengal's Sundarbans. Each operation offered lessons in mapping affected areas, locating stranded communities and improving the software used to plan missions. "It's not just a camera drone being flown and then dropping food material somewhere," says Kanu. "The most important thing is that it has to be effective, and that comes only when you have the data." The drones also conducted aerial surveys, helping rescue teams identify people stranded on rooftops and locate areas requiring urgent assistance. He explains that repeated field deployments have helped the team improve how it analyses affected areas and identifies locations that should be prioritised. The goal is to reduce the time between identifying a need and delivering assistance. The company's work extends beyond floods , too. Drones Tech Lab has worked with the Kolkata Municipal Corporation on dengue-control and medicine-spraying operations, supported aerial monitoring and surveillance at Kaziranga National Park, and undertaken healthcare logistics work with AIIMS using payload drones. Each of these applications requires the team to adapt its software, equipment and flight operations to the work being done on the ground. How can drones reach people faster next time? The work also draws on the ecosystem around IIT Guwahati, where Professor Parameshwar K. Iyer is associated with the Centre for Drone Technology. Iyer says efforts to strengthen the region's drone ecosystem gained momentum during the pandemic, when disaster management discussions highlighted the need for interdisciplinary solutions. Facilities for testing drones and training pilots became an important part of that effort. IIT Guwahati established designated areas for drone testing and operations, helping create infrastructure for companies and researchers working in the Northeast. The importance of having this infrastructure in place became clear during the recent Assam floods, when the response had to move quickly. After discussions with the team and state authorities, the drones and personnel were sent to Sivasagar overnight. Within 24 hours, the team was on the ground, surveying affected areas and helping identify stranded residents. For Iyer, the larger question is how such capabilities can be made available before the next emergency. "We have to be ready for any kind of disaster," he says. For communities cut off by floodwaters, drones offered a way to receive essential supplies and help rescue teams locate people waiting for assistance. Photograph: ( Hindustan Times ) He believes establishing drone facilities and services at multiple locations across vulnerable regions could reduce response times and help assistance reach communities faster. Such preparedness would require coordination between technology providers, local administrations and disaster-management agencies. Drones cannot replace evacuation teams, medical care or the wider relief network communities depend on. They can, however, help responders understand what is happening in areas that are difficult to reach and deliver limited supplies while further assistance is organised. 'They had lost hope of receiving relief' For Kanu, the impact of the Assam deployment was best understood through the reactions of people receiving help, rather than the distances flown or the weight carried by the drones. He remembers how some residents had lost hope of receiving relief because no one could easily reach them. Seeing supplies arrive by drone was an unfamiliar experience. "They had actually lost hope of receiving relief because they had no access to it," he says. "When we look back at the work we have put into building this company over the past 10 years, moments like these show us why we started. We may be sitting in Calcutta, working on technology day and night, but seeing it reach people who need help makes that journey worthwhile." As disasters continue to test communities and emergency services, drones offer one way to bridge the gap between those who need help and those trying to reach them. How effectively they can do this depends on their ability to work alongside relief teams on the ground. In Assam, technology developed over nearly a decade found an urgent purpose: carrying essential supplies across flooded terrain to people waiting for help. The next step is ensuring that when roads disappear again, the teams, infrastructure and coordination needed to respond are already in place. The team's efforts brought essential supplies and hope to communities cut off by the floods. For Dakshina, the experience is reason enough to make the technology available in more places. She hopes drones can help locate people and animals in danger and direct assistance towards areas that remain difficult to access. "I sincerely hope that such systems and technologies will be made available in more places," she says. All images courtesy Drones Tech Lab team
