items.descriptionOriginal: Note: A trip to the hills can offer a welcome change from the haze, traffic, and polluted air of a busy city. But while a few days amid greener surroundings may give you a breather, travelling cannot be a permanent solution to the problem of air pollution. Hill towns, too, experience changing air quality, and their clean-air promise should never be taken for granted. If you are planning a getaway, however, these five hill stations are worth considering. Just remember to check their latest AQI before you set off. As winter approaches, the skies above several cities begin to look different. A familiar haze settles over buildings, traffic moves beneath a blanket of smog, and stepping outdoors becomes uncomfortable. For people living in crowded urban centres, even a morning walk can mean spending time in polluted air. It is little surprise that the hills begin to look inviting at this time of the year. With forest trails, open landscapes, and fewer vehicles than in major cities, mountain towns offer a different environment . But does travelling to the hills actually mean breathing cleaner air? Not necessarily. Tourism, road construction, traffic, and seasonal weather conditions can affect air quality even in smaller hill towns. Looking at local AQI readings, rather than assuming that every green destination has clean air, can help travellers make a more informed choice. Here are five hill destinations to consider, along with their latest available air quality readings. 1. Landour, Uttarakhand For Delhi residents looking for a mountain escape, Landour offers a suitable alternative to the crowded streets of Mussoorie. Situated above the popular hill station, this small cantonment town is surrounded by oak and deodar forests, with walking trails and old colonial-era buildings. For Delhi residents looking for a mountain escape, Landour offers a suitable alternative to the crowded streets of Mussoorie. Photograph: (Hire A Camp) Visitors can explore the Circular Road, stop at Char Dukan for a cup of tea, or walk towards Lal Tibba, one of the area's best-known viewpoints. Its slower pace and forested surroundings make it appealing to travellers who prefer a peaceful break over a packed sightseeing itinerary. AccuWeather's latest dated reading available for Landour was 85 on 6 November 2026, classified as Poor on its air quality scale. 2. Gangtok, Sikkim For those willing to travel further from Kolkata, Gangtok offers a Himalayan alternative. Located at approximately 1,650 metres, the Sikkimese capital combines mountain views with monasteries, local markets, and natural surroundings. For those willing to travel further from Kolkata, Gangtok offers a Himalayan alternative. Photograph: (Travel India) Visitors can explore Rumtek Monastery, walk along MG Marg or take a trip to Tsomgo Lake. The surrounding mountain landscape also offers opportunities to experience Sikkim's local culture and food. On 6 November 2026, Gangtok recorded an AQI of 33 , classified as Good under India's AQI scale. The reading came from the Zero Point GICI monitoring station under the Sikkim State Pollution Control Board. 3. Madikeri, Karnataka Bengaluru residents looking for a change of environment can head to Madikeri in Kodagu, a region known for its coffee plantations, forest patches, and waterfalls. Visitors can explore Abbey Falls, located around eight kilometres from Madikeri, or head to Raja's Seat for views of the surrounding valleys. Coffee estate stays also offer an opportunity to walk through plantations and learn about how coffee is grown. Bengaluru residents looking for a change of environment can head to Madikeri in Kodagu. Photograph: (INIKA Resorts) On 6 November 2026, Madikeri recorded an AQI of 22 , classified as Good. The reading came from the Stuart Hill monitoring station operated by the Karnataka State Pollution Control Board. The station recorded a 24-hour AQI range of 3-28. 4. Chikkamagaluru, Karnataka Known for its coffee-growing landscape, Chikkamagaluru offers another mountain escape for people looking to spend time away from Bengaluru's busy roads. One of its highlights is Mullayanagiri, Karnataka's highest peak. Visitors can also explore Kemmangundi, which is surrounded by forests, mountain streams, and gardens. The surrounding coffee estates provide another way to experience the region. Chikkamagaluru offers another mountain escape for people looking to spend time away from Bengaluru's busy roads. Photograph: (Cozycozy) On 6 November 2026, Chikkamagaluru recorded an AQI of 38 , placing it in the Good category. The reading came from the Kalyana Nagara monitoring station. 5. Coonoor, Tamil Nadu Coonoor, in the Nilgiri Hills, is a peaceful alternative to Ooty for travellers who want to experience the mountains without spending their entire holiday in a busy tourist centre. The hill town is known for its tea-covered slopes and scenic railway journey. Visitors can explore Sim's Park, walk through tea estates or visit viewpoints such as Lamb's Rock and Dolphin's Nose. Coonoor, in the Nilgiri Hills, is a peaceful alternative to Ooty for travellers. Photograph: (Nilgiris Explorers) On 6 November 2026, AccuWeather reported an AQI of 11 for Coonoor, placing it in the Excellent category on its own scale. Can the hills really offer cleaner air? Travelling to the hills can mean spending less time around congested roads and dense urban development, but a lower AQI is never guaranteed. Weather conditions, tourist traffic, construction, and local pollution sources can change readings from one day to another. According to the Central Pollution Control Board, an AQI between 0 and 50 falls in the Good category, while 51 to 100 is considered Satisfactory. It is also important to check which AQI scale a platform uses. India's CPCB index and international indices can have different categories and breakpoints, so their numbers cannot always be compared directly. Before planning a trip , check the latest readings and identify the monitoring station or data source behind them. Choosing accommodation away from busy roads and exploring quieter parts of a destination can also help. The hills cannot promise pollution-free air. But checking the numbers before travelling can help you make a more informed choice about where to spend your next break.

items.title: The Spark: Όταν οι κοινότητες κατέχουν τη γη, η στέγαση παραμένει προσιτή
items.titleOriginal: The Spark: When Communities Own the Land, Housing Stays Affordable
items.description: Καλώς ήρθατε πίσω στο The Spark, τη μηνιαία γιορτή μας για το πώς άνθρωποι σαν εσάς δημιουργούν θετικές αλλαγές, ένα σημαντικό βήμα τη φορά. Το Spark υποστηρίζεται γενναιόδωρα από τη Laura Rice. Εγγραφείτε στο Reasons to be το εβδομαδιαίο ενημερωτικό δελτίο του Cheerful εδώ και θα λαμβάνετε το The Spark στα εισερχόμενά σας στην αρχή κάθε μήνα. Σε αυτό το τεύχος The power of communit…
items.descriptionOriginal: Welcome back to The Spark, our monthly celebration of how people just like you are creating positive change, one meaningful step at a time. The Spark is generously supported by Laura Rice. Sign up to Reasons to be Cheerful’s weekly newsletter here and you’ll get The Spark in your inbox at the start of each month. In this issue The power of community land trusts Cool roofs, cooler homes The perks of intergenerational roommates A community takes back its land In 2019, Nachand Trabue began noticing investors’ “We buy houses” signs all over her corner of Louisville, Kentucky. A historically Black neighborhood since the Civil War, Smoketown has deep roots and a long, proud past — including the city’s first Black library and first Black dentist, and as the birthplace of Muhammed Ali. But increasingly, long-term residents were getting priced out of their own community. For those like Trabue, a fourth-generation resident who remembered Smoketown in its thriving heyday, the change in their community was especially galling. “Because they’re taking away everything that made Smoketown great. They’re buying up the parks, the vacant lots, and putting in houses. There’s nothing for the kids. There’s no enrichment, no activity,” says Theresa Boyd, executive director of Smoketown Community Land Trust. A mural in Smoketown by The Art of Kacy. Credit: Don Sniegowski Trabue had had enough — she started pulling out the investors’ signs, reached out to the city’s land bank to figure out which vacant lots in the neighborhood were held by the city and connected with River City Housing , a local nonprofit home developer, to see how they could work together. At the same time, “the Smoketown Originals started to come together,” says Boyd, referring to a community organization of older residents with deep roots in the neighborhood. “They went to the churches, the community centers, the youth centers.” They started pushing the city to do a housing needs assessment and got in touch with Grounded Solutions , a national nonprofit for affordable housing, to decide whether a community land trust would be a viable option. Community land trusts (CLTs) are grassroots nonprofits that provide long-term affordable housing by buying and developing land on behalf of the community. When selling or renting homes, the CLT retains ownership of the land they’re built on, which makes the homes cheaper and keeps the land itself under community control. Crucially, CLTs also preserve affordability long-term by requiring owners to sell at an affordable price. The first CLTs grew out of the civil rights movement to secure land ownership for Black farmers. Today, they are an increasingly popular way of protecting land from speculators and creating long-term affordable housing, with over 300 CLTs in the US . The CLT’s first houses were recently completed, and more plots have already been chosen. Courtesy of Smoketown CLT In Smoketown, a lot of the initial work focused on explaining what a CLT is and getting the broader community on board. “Communities that have been divested [from] and have been talked to and at versus with, they lose their voice,” says Boyd. “We really had to rally the troops here in the community to be like, ‘You actually have a say in what goes on in your community.’” In 2020 the community and its partner organizations won the city’s Request for Proposals, securing $2.1 million to create a CLT. By 2023 the CLT was formalized and Boyd was brought onboard as the executive director. “I really whipped us into shape administratively and organizationally,” she says. “But most importantly, I went back out into the community and I was like, ‘Okay, this is what you wanted. Now what are we going to do with this land?’” Weighed down by negative news? Enter your email below to receive our smart, uplifting newsletters. Or click here to choose exactly which ones you want [contact-form-7] Based on a series of surveys, Smoketown CLT built its first seven houses right across the street from where Muhammed Ali threw his first punches under the watchful eye of trainer Fred Stoner, the grandfather of the CLT board president. These houses were recently completed, and the next seven plots have already been chosen. Before starting new developments, the CLT approaches the people living around the plots, says Boyd. “We invite them to the table: Okay, what are your concerns? What are your comments? This is what we are thinking. Is it a viable housing option for your street?” CLTs come in many different shapes, sizes and funding arrangements. In Smoketown, the CLT is funding the construction of the houses, but received the plots of land for free from the city. The land bank has earmarked around 70 plots in the neighborhood for the trust, says Boyd: “We were fortunate that those that came before me had enough gall to go to the city and be like, “Y’all holding all this land and you are absolutely not going to give it to investors. You are going to earmark it for the Community Land Trust.’ And we made them put it in writing.” Mayor Craig Greenberg joined Smoketown CLT to celebrate the completion of the CLT’s first seven homes. Courtesy of Smoketown CLT The city government has been supportive of the CLT, says Boyd, but it would not have happened without the community putting years of work into it. “Louisville’s been around for a really long time, and the people in our community absolutely will hold them to task, and that’s absolutely what they did. They started showing up at the council meetings, the reallocation of funds.” Partnering with experts, like Grounded Solutions, is key to getting a CLT off the ground, as is ensuring that community members see themselves represented in the CLT leadership, says Boyd. “[And] you have to be willing to change and really meet people where they are and not be afraid to make good trouble.” Learn more about Smoketown Community Land Trust here , or get additional information from Grounded Solutions here . Keeping it cool one roof at a time When Tony Chaves noticed how extreme heat and rising air-conditioning costs were affecting his Las Vegas neighborhood, he decided to help solve the problem with a ladder and a bucket of ultra-reflective white paint. As part of the two-person nonprofit Alchemical Opus, Chavez started painting the roofs of Arts District businesses for free, significantly decreasing their indoor temperatures, with one business owner reporting saving $60 to $70 a month on electricity. Coating roofs in white paint is an easy way to lower the temperatures of homes and public buildings. In recent years homeowners across India, Burkina Faso, Mexico and South Pacific have painted their roofs white as part of a global scientific study, with early results indicating substantial cooling. In the U.S., Philadelphia gave 62 households free cool-roof coatings in a 2025 pilot project, while the New York City CoolRoofs program has painted over 12 million square feet of roofs with reflective white paint since 2007. A number of U.S. cities also require cool roofs on new and re-roofed buildings. Wait, you're not a member yet? Join the Reasons to be Cheerful community by supporting our nonprofit publication and giving what you can. Join Cancel anytime The science behind the idea is straightforward: White and reflective roofs absorb less solar heat, and applying reflective coatings is the easiest way to transform a roof into a so-called “cool roof,” while also prolonging the life of the roof . The U.S. Department of Energy says cool roofs can reduce annual air-conditioning energy use in single-story buildings by up to 15 percent, while other studies show that painted roofs can lower maximum indoor temperatures by 2.2 to 5.9°F in residential buildings that are not air conditioned. Learn more about cool roofs here . Housing across generations After moving from the countryside to Vienna for university, Lukas Hecke, Manuel Schuler and Marlene Welzl experienced first-hand how difficult it could be to find good housing on a student budget. At the same time, they knew the city was full of elderly people with small pensions and large apartments, who often felt lonely after their children grew up and moved out. In 2015 they started connecting older people with spare rooms to younger people looking for a place to live. It began organically, by word of mouth, and soon grew into the housing platform Wohnbuddy that has carefully matched over 400 people based on their interests and communications over the years. The impact goes beyond private homes. Since 2017, Wohnbuddy has also partnered with senior residences, where students bring new energy through activities, music and social interaction. Learn more about Wohnbuddy here . The post The Spark: When Communities Own the Land, Housing Stays Affordable appeared first on Reasons to be Cheerful .

items.descriptionOriginal: Northwestern University reports that "over 3,000 newspapers have closed in the U.S. in the past 20 years." It not only means limited access to local news, but job loss for staff who live in and have long-term relationships with the community. Academic institutions such as Northwestern are working with students to either rescue legacy newspapers or start new publications focused on serving the community over profit. Students and academic staff work together to provide the journalism for the community while students earn credits or internships. "While the student newspaper office is inside the journalism school's building, it operates independently." One journalism school director said, "They know these communities. So that was really important just from a moral and ethical imperative, but also from a news perspective," she said. "They're trusted in their communities. They know what's going on."

Γεννημένη στο Thrissur της Κεράλα, η Nithya πέρασε τα πρώτα της χρόνια στο Thiruvananthapuram πριν μετακομίσει στις ΗΠΑ με την οικογένειά της περίπου…
items.descriptionOriginal: Description: She just made history as Los Angeles’ first South Asian mayor-elect! Kerala-born Nithya Raman defeated incumbent Karen Bass with 52.1% of the vote. But her journey to this moment began thousands of miles away. Born in Thrissur, Kerala, Nithya spent her early years in Thiruvananthapuram before moving to the US with her family at around six. After graduating from Harvard in 2003, she returned to India to work with communities often left out of urban development plans. In Delhi, she supported slum residents facing eviction ahead of the 2010 Commonwealth Games. In Chennai, she founded Transparent Chennai, using data mapping to make civic issues in underserved neighbourhoods visible to policymakers. After earning a master’s in urban planning from MIT, she moved to Los Angeles, working on housing and homelessness. In 2020, she entered politics, winning a seat on LA’s City Council. She was re-elected in 2024. Now, she is set to lead the city. She once worked to make overlooked communities heard. Now, she has a city of millions listening. ❤️ #WomenInPolitics #IndianWomen #NithyaRaman #LosAngelesMayor #WomenInPolitics #Kerala #IndianInspiration #Thrissur #InidaninUSA #UrbanPlanning #WomenWhoLead #IndianDiaspora #MadeHistory #TheBetterIndia

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Protecting Congo Basin Peatlands Gets a Scientific Boost Reading Time: 3 minutes A major research collection on African tropical peatlands provides new scientific backing for protecting Congo Basin peatlands and strengthens UNEP’s conservation efforts. A major research collection published in September provides new scientific backing for protecting Congo Basin peatlands . The special issue, released in the Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B, brings together studies on the ecology, hydrology, and social dimensions of African tropical peatlands. Much of the research centers on the Cuvette Centrale, the vast peat swamp spanning the Republic of Congo and the Democratic Republic of Congo. Scientists first mapped the full extent of these peatlands in 2017, revealing a wetland larger than England hidden deep in the Congo Basin’s swamp forests. Researchers estimated the area holds roughly 30 billion metric tons of carbon, an amount comparable to about three years of global fossil fuel emissions. That discovery reshaped how researchers think about tropical peatlands’ role in regulating the planet’s carbon cycle. Keeping that carbon locked underground depends entirely on the peat staying wet. Drainage, agricultural conversion, or sustained drought could release large amounts of stored carbon dioxide back into the atmosphere. Protecting Congo Basin peatlands therefore hinges less on stopping any single threat and more on preserving the hydrological conditions that keep the peat intact. The new research collection highlights how much remains unknown about these dynamics. Contributors point to persistent gaps in understanding how the peatlands might respond to future shifts in rainfall, temperature, and land use. Closing those gaps has become a priority for governments and international partners working across the region. International attention around the peatlands has grown steadily since their 2017 discovery. In 2018, the Republic of Congo, the Democratic Republic of Congo, and Indonesia signed a joint declaration committing to protect their peatlands from unregulated development. The agreement built on momentum from the Global Peatlands Initiative, which has pushed peatland protection higher on the global policy agenda. That cooperation extends beyond the three signatory countries themselves. Researchers and policymakers from outside the region have increasingly framed protecting Congo Basin peatlands as a shared international responsibility, given how much global climate stability depends on keeping the carbon in place. Scientific exchange between African, European, and Asian institutions has become a regular feature of that ongoing collaboration. Protecting Congo Basin peatlands has evolved into a shared international responsibility, with the Republic of Congo, DRC, and Indonesia’s 2018 joint declaration and growing scientific collaboration between African, European, and Asian institutions reflecting global recognition that the climate stability of the entire planet depends on keeping this carbon in the ground. Photo courtesy of the UN Environment Programme . Much of the scientific groundwork behind that cooperation comes from research programs such as CongoPeat, led by the University of Leeds. The project has mapped peat extent and carbon stocks across the central Congo Basin while studying how the ecosystem has formed and changed over thousands of years. That evidence base now feeds directly into regional conservation planning. Translating that science into action falls largely to the Congo Basin Landscapes Initiative, a UNEP-led effort working with regional governments and partners. Within that framework, a dedicated peatlands project backed by Germany’s International Climate Initiative is supporting work in the Lac Télé–Lac Tumba landscape. The project represents nearly €15 million in funding between 2022 and 2027. One tool developed under the project models how different development and climate scenarios could affect water levels and carbon storage across the landscape. Results consistently point to the same conclusion: altering drainage patterns carries real risks for the carbon locked in peat. That finding reinforces why protecting Congo Basin peatlands depends so heavily on careful land-use planning. Research led by the University of Leeds shows the peatlands remain mostly intact today, though threats from road building, logging, and resource extraction continue to grow around their edges. Keeping that intact status will require sustained funding and coordination well beyond any single research project or funding cycle. Protecting Congo Basin peatlands adds another layer of evidence to that ongoing effort rather than offering a final answer. Protecting one of the world’s largest carbon stores will continue to depend on scientists, governments, and local communities working from the same shared body of knowledge. For the Congo Basin, that sustained collaboration may matter as much as any single policy or funding commitment. The post Protecting Congo Basin Peatlands Gets a Scientific Boost appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.title: Μια ενδιάμεση στάση σε μια παγκόσμια διαδρομή πουλιών: Πώς ο υγρότοπος Sukhna του Chandigarh διατηρεί την απειλούμενη άγρια ​​ζωή
items.titleOriginal: A Stopover on a Global Bird Route: How Chandigarh’s Sukhna Wetland Sustains Threatened Wildlife
items.description: Ο εμβληματικός υγρότοπος Sukhna του Chandigarh έχει οριστεί επίσημα ως η 103η τοποθεσία Ramsar της Ινδίας. Ο υγρότοπος έχει λάβει τον αριθμό τοποθεσίας 2602, τοποθετώντας το Chandigarh στον παγκόσμιο χάρτη των διεθνώς αναγνωρισμένων υγροτόπων. Στην άκρη του Chandigarh, όπου οι λόφοι Shivalik υψώνονται προς τα Ιμαλάια, η λίμνη Sukhna προσφέρει στους κατοίκους περισσότερο από μια έκταση…
items.descriptionOriginal: Chandigarh's iconic Sukhna Wetland has been officially designated as India's 103rd Ramsar Site. The wetland has been assigned Site Number 2602, placing Chandigarh on the global map of internationally recognised wetlands. On the edge of Chandigarh, where the Shivalik Hills rise towards the Himalayas, Sukhna Lake offers residents more than a stretch of open water. Its banks, surrounding vegetation and adjoining woodland form habitats that sustain wildlife, including birds that travel thousands of kilometres between continents. The lake serves as a feeding, breeding, roosting, and wintering ground for migratory waterbirds. Photograph: (Unpetitprole) Sukhna is a peri-urban reservoir. This means it is a waterbody located within or near an urban area, while still performing important ecological functions. Now, this ecological importance has received international recognition. Four habitats, one interconnected ecosystem A wetland is not simply an expanse of water. Its ecological character depends on the different habitats that exist within and around it, and these habitats allow different forms of wildlife to use the wetland in different ways. Some species depend on the open water, while others use the vegetation along the banks or the surrounding woodland. This diversity is particularly important for birds that use Sukhna as a seasonal stopover. For migratory waterbirds, wetlands are not isolated destinations. They form part of larger geographical routes connecting breeding grounds, feeding areas and wintering habitats. A stop along the Central Asian Flyway Sukhna lies along the Central Asian Flyway , a major migratory route used by birds travelling between their breeding and non-breeding grounds. During these journeys, birds need suitable places to feed, rest and recover before continuing their migration. Wetlands such as Sukhna provide these essential habitats. The lake serves as a feeding, breeding, roosting, and wintering ground for migratory waterbirds. Each of these functions matters at a different stage of a bird's life cycle. Sukhna also supports species with different conservation statuses, highlighting the importance of protecting its habitats. India's Ramsar Site network grows to 103! With Sukhna Lake in Chandigarh and Sauj Jheel in Uttar Pradesh joining the list, India's commitment to wetland conservation continues to grow. These wetlands conserve biodiversity, strengthen water and climate security, and sustain local livelihoods. Their recognition also reinforces the importance of protecting these vital ecosystems for future generations. #AmritDharohar — MoEF&CC (@moefcc) October 15, 2026 Three notable species associated with the wetland include: Common Pochard: Classified as Vulnerable, this diving duck depends on suitable freshwater habitats. Pallas's Fish Eagle: Classified as Endangered, this large raptor is associated with wetland and riverine ecosystems. Black Pond Turtle: Classified as Endangered, this freshwater turtle depends on suitable aquatic environments for its survival. What does the Ramsar designation mean? The Ramsar Convention is an international agreement for the conservation and wise use of wetlands. Named after the Iranian city where it was adopted in 1971, it provides a framework for recognising wetlands that are important at an international level. Being included on the Ramsar List brings international recognition to a wetland's ecological significance and draws attention to the need for its conservation. With Sukhna's inclusion, India's Ramsar network now stands at 103 sites. For Chandigarh, the designation places one of its important urban wetlands within this international conservation framework. Its new status is therefore more than an international listing . It is recognition that even within a planned city, a wetland can remain part of a much larger ecological network, connecting local landscapes with wildlife and migratory routes that extend far beyond national boundaries. Sources: 'India's Ramsar Site tally reaches 103 with addition of Sukhna Wetland (Chandigarh) and Sauj Jheel (UP)' : By PIB Delhi, Published on 15 October 2026 'The Ramsar Sites Criteria-The nine criteria for identifying Wetlands of International Importance' : By Ramsar Convention on Wetlands 'Sukhna Lake-Chandigarh' : Chandigarh Tourism

items.descriptionOriginal: Picture a small workshop in Goa, barely large enough to turn around in. A furnace glows in one corner, the air thick with heat and the faint metallic smell of melting gold. An artisan bends over a workbench, a single sharpened wire in hand, and begins to carve a name into a ring, stroke by careful stroke, with no machine to help him. This is the world Prachi Shirodkar spent months filming for her documentary Bhaangar Kalakusar Karigiri , a world she knew intimately because her own father and grandfather had once worked in it. The 28-year-old directed, shot and narrated the documentary , handling the filming herself, while her father wrote the script and her partner edited the film. 'Lockdown changed all my plans' Shirodkar was one year into a B.Arch degree in 2020 when the country went into lockdown. Lockdown in 2020 prompted Prachi Shirodkar to leave architecture behind and discover her calling in storytelling. With classes paused and the world outside shut down, she found herself alone with her thoughts for the first time in years. "When you're by yourself, that's when you really get to know yourself," she says of that period. What she discovered was that design had never been the thing pulling at her . Storytelling was, and always had been. She had grown up around theatre and acting, but with no one in her family from the film or media industry, architecture had felt like the safer, more familiar choice after school. The lockdown gave her room to reconsider, and she switched to mass communication instead. "This was my element," she tells The Better India. "I am myself. I know what I'm doing, and I love it." Her father's script, her camera & a story rooted in Goa For her final-year project, Shirodkar turned the camera on the goldsmiths she had grown up watching at work. "I'm not trying to represent the community here; it's about their art and their skill," she says of her intention. With no filmmaking experience or fixed schedule, Shirodkar began documenting artisans she had known since childhood. Photograph: (Still from the film) She also made a deliberate choice to include women artisans in the film. "It's not just men who do this anymore," she says. Making the film in Konkani was never really a decision at all. "I am Goan, this is happening in Goa, and Konkani is my mother tongue. I didn't have to think twice," she says, noting that even within the language, the dialects of Mapsa, Pernem and Margao carry their own small differences. Her father, who had worked in the trade himself, wrote the film's script in that specific vocabulary, giving her a foundation to build the film around. Her father's experience in goldsmithing shaped the documentary's Konkani script, preserving the trade's vocabulary and cultural roots. The project almost didn't happen. It began as a college group assignment that fell through when the group arrangement did not work out, and Shirodkar shelved it, intending to return to it only after graduation. It was her partner, Mario Pimenta, who convinced her to pick it back up. "It was his idea. I'm grateful he pushed for it," she says. He went on to edit the film while she handled the filming, direction and narration herself, despite having never operated a camera before. There was no fixed shoot schedule and barely any budget. "Whatever I had in hand was what mattered," she says of how she funded it. Shoots depended entirely on when her subjects, many of them relatives and family friends she had known for years, happened to be free. A goldsmith engraving an entire name with a slender wire revealed the remarkable precision behind the traditional craft. This meant filming in scattered bursts across several weeks rather than in one continuous run. Piecing together a coherent narrative from those fragments was one of the hardest parts of the process. "I kept asking myself whether I had the flow right or was missing something," she recalls. One moment stayed with her long after the shoot ended: a craftsman engraving a name into gold with nothing but a slim metal wire. "It doesn't even look like a knife; it looks like a wire," she says. "He carved the entire name using just that. Our hands are so skilled." 'You have a camera, you have a story' The film's festival run began with rejections. Then came an unexpected first selection at Jackson Doc Fest in Tennessee, USA, followed by screenings in Kerala at the International Folklore Film Festival and a selection for the International Cultural Journal Award in Uzhhorod, Ukraine. It also won Best Documentary at the Miseentage Indian Film Awards, and Shirodkar was recently conferred a Young Achievers Award by Rotary International for her contribution to culture. "They just called out my name, and I was genuinely taken aback," she says of the moment. Shirodkar filmed the artisans herself, while her partner Mario Pimenta edited the footage into a cohesive story of Goa's goldsmithing tradition. She now works as an assistant director in Mumbai, and the scale of commercial production has reshaped how she thinks about her own filmmaking. "What you learn in theory is so different from what happens in practice," she says, adding that if she made the film again today, she would write a fuller script and bring in a dedicated cinematographer rather than shoot it herself. Her advice to other young filmmakers starting out without money or a team is blunt and repeated often in conversation: find people you trust, however small the crew. "If you have the right people with you, everything will fall into place," she says. Do not let the absence of a budget stop you from starting. Now an assistant director in Mumbai, Shirodkar urges young filmmakers to begin with the stories closest to home. "There are filmmakers who have made it happen with very little money, and they've done so well," she says. "You have a camera, you have a story. Just go shoot it." And look close to home first, she adds, because the most powerful subjects are often the ones already around you. "Start from where you belong, and then go step by step."

items.description: ΑΠΟ ΤΗΝ ΚΑΘΗΜΕΡΙΝΗ ΣΥΝΤΑΚΤΙΚΗ ΟΜΑΔΑ OPTIMIST Κάθε πρωί στον καταυλισμό στο Teknaf, στο Μπαγκλαντές, ο Mohammed Saber ανεβαίνει στην οροφή του σπιτιού της οικογένειάς του από μπαμπού και μουσαμά και τοποθετεί ένα ενιαίο ορθογώνιο ηλιακό πάνελ. Το έκανε αυτό για έξι χρόνια, από τότε που η οικογένειά του διέφυγε από την καταστολή των Ροχίνγκια από τον στρατό της Μιανμάρ το 2017. «Μπορούμε τώρα να χρεώσουμε…
items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Every morning in the camp at Teknaf, Bangladesh, Mohammed Saber climbs to the roof of his family’s bamboo-and-tarpaulin home and sets out a single rectangular solar panel. He has done this for six years, since his family fled the Myanmar military’s crackdown on the Rohingya people in 2017. “We can now charge our phones, cook with light, children can study at night and use fans during the hot season,” says Saber, 35. A small panel on a makeshift roof, and an entire household runs on it. The same thing is happening in camps and disaster zones around the world. Solar has been edging into humanitarian response for years; what’s shifted is how seriously organizations are taking it, less as an experiment and more as something people actually need. From lanterns to cook stoves The range of what “solar kit” means is wider than it might sound. Sarah Rosenberg-Jansen , a research fellow at the Stockholm Environment Institute , describes the category as spanning solar lanterns, torches, and heating pads to full solar home systems and electric cook stoves . The common thread is portability and independence from the grid, which matters most when infrastructure is gone and things are moving fast. “In emergency situations , solar kits can be deployed immediately,” she says. That’s playing out across multiple places at once. In Karachi, Doctors Without Borders runs a tuberculosis clinic on solar power. In South Sudan’s Renk County , the UN migration agency installed solar-powered water filtration for families displaced by the war in neighboring Sudan. When Nepal’s floods killed 1,455 people and left 5,285 missing in August, local and international organizations distributed solar kits to survivors cut off from the grid. In Ukraine, a nonprofit called Hope For Ukraine has provided kits to thousands of families living through a war, including older residents who adapted without trouble. “We have grandmas and grandpas who are around 75 to 80 years old receiving kits,” says CEO Yuriy Boyechko. “It’s just a matter of plug and play.” Why costs finally shifted Solar panels don’t carry the same price volatility as fossil fuels, which are expensive and difficult to transport into disaster zones under ordinary circumstances and near-impossible when infrastructure has been destroyed. Only a few decades ago, solar was a luxury technology. Mass manufacturing and steady advances in efficiency changed that, and the price drop put solar kits within reach of humanitarian budgets in ways they weren’t before. Funding cuts and the waiting list What’s slowing things down now isn’t the technology. Aid organizations have long-running contracts built around diesel generators, and switching to solar means trusting new equipment, building new distribution chains, and sometimes doing that in genuinely hazardous conditions. Mark Gibson of the Global Platform for Action , a group promoting clean energy access, notes that the transition has been complicated for organizations with established logistics in place. Cuts to international donor funding have made it harder. Aimee Jenks, a program leader at GPA, was direct: “Much of the technical expertise in the humanitarian sector on energy has been cut. That’s now retracting a lot of progress.” Hope For Ukraine’s own numbers show how stretched the system is. By the end of 2026, the organization expects to have distributed more than 3,200 solar kits, a number that took two years to reach because of funding. “We have a waiting list of about 20,000 families,” Boyechko says. “We just cannot keep up with demand.” For Saber, the gap between what’s available and what people have isn’t an abstraction. His family has had their panel for six years, long enough to know exactly what changed. “It’s improved my family’s life,” he says. Did this solution stand out? items.descriptionOriginal: The U.K.’s first “Flower Pharmacy” opened its doors last month — prescribing bouquets instead of medicine to those in need of a mood boost. The one-off experience in London was designed to encourage people to think differently about flowers, showing how they can play a role in everyday well-being rather than just being reserved for birthdays, anniversaries, and other special occasions. It was created in partnership with Plants and Flowers Foundation Holland and chartered horticulturist, TV gardener, and author David Domoney. Guests were matched with blooms tailored to their mood before leaving with a bouquet recommended to lift, calm, or energize them. For example, yellow flowers, including sunflowers, roses, freesias, and snapdragons, were prescribed to boost happiness, while calming bouquets featured blue and green blooms like hydrangeas, delphiniums, and chrysanthemums. For those who needed a dose of energy, there were also vibrant orange, red, and pink flowers. Courtesy of SWNS The event came as a poll of 2,000 British adults found 37% struggle when daylight saving time ends, with 29% admitting the time change leaves them feeling glum. Discussing the partnership with Plants and Flowers Foundation Holland, which commissioned the research and the pop-up, Domoney said: “There’s something incredibly uplifting about flowers, and research has shown that they can have a positive effect on our mood and emotional well-being. From the cheerful yellows of sunflowers and freesias to the calming tones of blues and greens, color can influence how we experience the spaces around us.” “We often associate flowers with special occasions, but there’s no reason we shouldn’t enjoy their beauty and the benefits of having them around us in everyday life,” he continued. “Sometimes, it’s the simplest connections with nature that can make a real difference to how we feel.” Courtesy of SWNS The survey also found that around a third of respondents spend more time indoors following the clock change, while 28% find the darker evenings difficult and 22% experience lower energy levels. The good news? There are plenty of ways to lift that low mood, like listening to music, reading a book, exercising, spending time in nature and, yes, buying flowers. While just 9% of people said they regularly treat themselves to blooms, the emotional response to receiving them is clear — half said they feel happy after being presented with a bouquet, 45% grateful, 34% joyful, and 24% comforted. Courtesy of SWNS Monique Kemperman, horticulture expert for Plants and Flowers Foundation Holland, said: “As the days become shorter and darker, small acts of self-care can make a real difference, and flowers are a simple way to bring color, joy, and positivity into everyday life.” “Our research shows just how much of an emotional impact they can have, yet many people still reserve them for somebody else or a special occasion,” she added. “The Flower Pharmacy is about encouraging people to see flowers as an everyday well-being boost rather than a treat.” This article was originally written by Jasmine Lenthall for SWNS — the U.K.’s largest independent news agency, providing globally relevant original, verified, and engaging content to the world’s leading media outlets.

items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM There’s a particular kind of motivation that kicks in around the holidays. You think: this year, I’m going to do something. You picture yourself in an apron at a soup kitchen, and it feels good. The problem is that a lot of other people are picturing the same thing at the same time. Most food banks and soup kitchens see volunteer demand spike around Thanksgiving , sometimes to the point where they have more help than they can use on that one day. If you want your time to count, a little strategy goes a long way. The good news: there are 17 solid options below, and several of them work whether you have four hours, four minutes, or no desire to leave your couch. National organizations with locations near you These programs operate across all 50 states, so wherever you are, there’s likely a chapter close enough to walk in. Feeding America Feeding America runs the largest hunger-relief network in the country. If you want to volunteer at a food bank on Thanksgiving, call ahead first. Holiday demand often fills slots fast, and some locations redirect walk-ins toward future dates when the need is more consistent. Meals on Wheels Meals on Wheels delivers hot meals to seniors who can’t get out on their own. The flexibility here is part of the appeal: you can sign up for a single delivery route or build it into a regular habit. The Salvation Army The Salvation Army works across a wide range of needs, from veterans to abuse survivors to people experiencing homelessness. There’s almost always something useful you can do, even on short notice. Operation Turkey Operation Turkey runs a tightly organized four-hour shift from 8 a.m. to noon, packing meals for homeless individuals. If you want a defined commitment with a clear end time, this is a good fit. Feed My Starving Children Feed My Starving Children packs meals at permanent sites in Arizona, Illinois, Minnesota, and Texas. It runs on a reservation system, so sign up before the week of. Toys for Tots Toys for Tots runs its drives through December, so Thanksgiving week is peak season. Volunteer slots exist for collection drives, not just drop-offs. Goodwill Goodwill often looks for people who can share a professional skill, not just sort donations. If you have a background in workforce development, finance, or career coaching, that’s where you’d fit in. United Way United Way sponsors a range of community initiatives, including garden planting, literacy programs, and neighborhood projects. What’s available depends on your city, so look up your local chapter. Local options that don’t require a national signup Soup kitchens and community meal programs often run on the same skeleton crew year after year. A call a week ahead is usually all it takes. Animal shelters are another option, especially if you’re better with dogs than crowds. Staff still work on Thanksgiving, and extra hands for walks or socialization are usually welcome. If you’re up for something more active, turkey trots are 5K races held in communities across the country on Thanksgiving morning, with proceeds going to local charities. You walk or run, and the entry fee does the work. The National Park Service also coordinates trail maintenance and cleanup projects throughout the fall. Check the volunteer page for your nearest park. If you can’t leave the house Gift-a-Family Gift-a-Family lets you sponsor a family through their holiday wishlist. The sign-up deadline is November 30, so there’s still time. Homefront America Homefront America directs donations toward grocery and turkey vouchers for military families. Support Our Troops Support Our Troops coordinates handwritten letters to deployed service members. It takes about ten minutes and goes a long way. One thing to know before you go Holiday volunteering is genuinely good, but the reality is that organizations often need year-round help. Of course, showing up once during the holidays could be the gateway to showing up regularly. If you get redirected on Thanksgiving Day because a food bank is at capacity, ask when they need people most. Often the answer is right after the holiday rush! Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary . The post The best places to volunteer this Thanksgiving: 17 options for every schedule first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News .

items.descriptionOriginal: T he staff at Erik’s Ranch & Retreats has a saying: Sheets, towels and lives changed daily . Erik’s Ranch is a guest retreat where autistic people are concierges, guides, wranglers, cooks and more. Located on 230 acres of pristine pasture and wilderness near Livingston, Montana, the ranch is less than an hour from Yellowstone National Park. It offers horseback riding, fly fishing, nature hikes, history walks and experiences with ranch animals and wildlife — most led or assisted by paid neurodivergent “members,” most of whom also live on the property. The inspiration for Erik’s Ranch dates back to 2008, when founder Kathryn Nordberg was pondering how her son, Erik, whom she described as “a moderately functioning teenager with autism,” would live as an adult — and particularly what would happen when she was no longer around. Ranch manager Cameron Porter (in black hat) and member John Rekedal help a visitor from New Jersey mount her steed for a trail ride. Credit: Jodi Hausen “As someone challenged with expressive language, there weren’t very many opportunities for kids like him,” she said, sitting in the well-appointed kitchen of the ranch’s six-bedroom lodge. So she established a nonprofit with a boutique-style hotel in Edina, Minnesota, where, even after she’s gone, Erik and others like him can live, work and thrive. There, adults on the autism spectrum work and live independently and are guided by life coaches toward achieving personal goals like interviewing, equine or cooking skills; or setting up an Etsy page to sell their artwork. Weighed down by negative news? Enter your email below to receive our smart, uplifting newsletters. Or click here to choose exactly which ones you want [contact-form-7] Using a similar model, in 2014 Nordberg opened the Montana ranch, where not only employees on the spectrum benefit: She designed most of the cabins specifically for neurodivergent guests. Though anyone can appreciate the soothing atmosphere, it’s particularly accommodating for those on the spectrum, who sometimes experience sensory overload. The calmingly simple cabins provide awe-inspiring vistas of the surrounding mountains with little to no sign of human activity. Hardware was selected to close drawers, cabinets and doors with hardly a sound. Walls, furnishings and bedding are muted earth tones and lights have dimmers. Credit: Jodi Hausen Erik’s Ranch is run primarily by young autistic people, some of whom also live on the property. The ranch has unparalleled views of the Absaroka-Beartooth Mountains. Autistic and other neurodivergent people are often misunderstood and feel out-of-place, experiencing discrimination, social exclusion, bullying and other situations that can lead to low self-esteem. That — and an inexorable need to mask their differences — often results in depression and anxiety. Some studies indicate that people on the spectrum are four times more likely to experience major depression compared with the general population. “Depression, loneliness, lack of confidence, feeling isolated, rejected, and a lack of community and people who care is what Erik’s Ranch is working to minimize and eliminate,” Nordberg said. And it’s working. John Rekedal, 21, lives in Minnesota but just spent his first summer working at the Montana ranch. When he’s home, he works in a large production greenhouse. And though his coworkers there are understanding, he prefers the camaraderie of working with the ranch’s small staff amid the hush of the surrounding mountains. Jacob Thoresen fetches horses from a pasture in preparation for a trail ride. Thoresen has been working for Erik’s Ranch and Retreats for 10 years. Credit: Jodi Hausen “I’m a whole lot more inclined to work outside,” he said. “And I know everyone’s name. It’s more relaxed.” Cornell University autism researcher Leslie Shaw analyzed a national sample of autistic adults who could answer a survey unassisted and found that only about 53 percent were working in 2023. Furthermore, in 2024, people with cognitive disabilities (of which neurodivergence is a subset) were employed at less than half the rate of people without any disability, according to Cornell’s Northeast ADA Center . These low employment rates may be due to neurotypical employers’ lack of experience with and understanding of neurodivergent people leading to misaligned work assignments, confusion and a fraught or untenable work environment. On a recent late summer day in Montana, Jacob Thoresen, 33, was gearing up to lead a small group of guests on a trail ride. He has been working with the nonprofit for 10 years and splits his time between its two locations. In black cowboy hat and jeans, he walked back and forth across the dirt-floored indoor arena to a tack room, gathering saddles and bridles. He saddled horses while other members dutifully scooped and cleaned areas around the animals. Credit: Jodi Hausen Erik’s Ranch & Retreats is part of a growing trend of workplaces designed to integrate people with autism or other disabilities. Thoresen had other jobs before coming to Erik’s. He was a baggage handler at the Minneapolis-Saint Paul Airport and worked in retail and manufacturing. He even tried a desk job. “But,” he said with a smile, “that isn’t me.” Thoresen said he’s gained confidence working with Erik’s Ranch & Retreats. “If you would have met me 10 years ago, I would have been, like, I couldn’t be able to do anything independent and be trusted to actually get the work done,” he said. “This place is teaching me how to be independent. In this last year, I’ve grown more.” He still gets support, but staff, recognizing his achievements, have loosened the reins. “I’m having to rely more on myself to work on those independent skills,” he added. Hannah Jacobs (left) helps Zoe Markman put fresh linens on a bed in one of the guest cabins at Erik’s Ranch. Credit: Jodi Hausen When asked what he finds challenging about working at Erik’s Ranch, Thoresen said workdays can be inconsistent. At the Minnesota retreat, he completes the same tasks daily. On the ranch, daily schedules shift and sometimes he gets overwhelmed. “But I can move through it,” he said. “I attribute that to the staff that I work with and just practice. They do a good job of seeing [my overwhelm] and being like, okay. And that helps, you know. I’ve had too many employers in the past that have been like, ‘Oh, you’re not having a good day? Well, just go home.’” Over the years, Erik’s Ranch & Retreats has employed 27 autistic young adults — 19 in the last year. The goal, Nordberg said, is to serve 30 members regularly. The organization is part of a growing trend of workplaces designed to integrate people with autism or other disabilities. John Rekedal helps clean around the horses in the indoor arena before a trail ride. Credit: Jodi Hausen Not far from Erik’s Ranch, Special K Ranch in Columbus, Montana, provides living quarters and jobs in farming, ranching and gardening and contracts with area businesses to employ adults with developmental disabilities. Over in Jackson, Wyoming, Vertical Harvest integrates people with a wide array of disabilities into their operations growing lettuces, microgreens, tomatoes and basil. In a fully accessible greenhouse, Vertical Harvest operates on what’s known as the “Grow Well” model of employment : providing opportunities for workers to pursue passions by creating or placing them in positions that correspond to their strengths and aspirations, their likes and dislikes. In other words, adapting the workplace to the employee rather than the other way around. Although she hadn’t heard of Grow Well, Nordberg embraces its philosophy. It doesn’t always work out as planned, though. “Not everyone wants to learn hospitality,” she said. In fact, one autistic young man told her he wanted to be a “white hat hacker,” using his computer skills for good. But she didn’t have a role that fit his skills and aspirations. In other instances, however, a member’s passions can be integrated into ranch operations. Part-time member Zoe Markman shows off a colorful collection of eggs gathered from the hens in the coop behind her. Credit: Jodi Hausen Zoe Markman, a 21-year-old autistic woman from Bozeman, loves animals — particularly chickens. So when Markman started working part-time at the ranch, Nordberg built a chicken coop and populated it with more than a dozen hens whom Markman gave punny names: Chiquille O’Neal, Princess Layer and Hen Solo. On a recent workday, Markman gathered more than a dozen colorful eggs. Nordberg also helped Erik start a baking business making cookies, brownies, scones and banana bread. Erik is a visual learner and communicator, so Nordberg created a pictorial cookbook with step-by-step instructions. She marked bins of flour, sugar and other ingredients with pictures so Erik can do most of the work independently. Wait, you're not a member yet? Join the Reasons to be Cheerful community by supporting our nonprofit publication and giving what you can. Join Cancel anytime The ranch can currently house five members and has five cabins and the lodge for guests on its expansive property. So Nordberg has room to expand, and she’d like to. But finances and land-use regulations present barriers. It’s expensive running a guest ranch, though the costs are partly covered by guest fees and philanthropy. And area permitting will only allow for seven more cabins. “This will never be a huge operation,” Nordberg said. But she’s gratified knowing there are places for Erik and others like him to live, belong and find meaningful work. This story was supported in part by the Solutions Journalism Network’s HEAL Fellowship. items.descriptionOriginal: Sewage is full of organic matter that can be a source of energy. But it also carries harmful chemicals as well as leftover medicines that conventional treatment methods can’t remove easily. Researchers now report a technology that can solve three sewage-related problems at the same time. Their new device uses bacteria in wastewater to generate electricity while breaking down a hard-to-degrade antibiotic and producing a valuable industrial chemical. The team published their results in Journal of Power Sources . There have been plenty of research efforts to harness microbes for treating wastewater while producing renewable energy. The approach uses microbial fuel cells , which are battery-like devices with two electrodes. In microbial fuel cells, bacteria grow on an electrode and devour organic matter , converting chemical energy into electrons, which flow in an external circuit to produce electricity. Then those electrons meet oxygen at the other electrode to create water. Turns out that microbial fuel cells usually generate very small amounts of electricity. “So we asked a different question: What else could those electrons do when they arrive?,” writes the team from both;} Recommended Reading: Designer bacteria clean wastewater and generate power—at the same time If all the electrons don’t combine with oxygen and hydrogen at the second electrode, the product is hydrogen peroxide instead of water. Hydrogen peroxide is a household chemical used for disinfection and bleaching. It is also used widely in chemical manufacturing. The chemical industry makes it today using an energy- and chemical-intensive process in large plants. To get the right reaction in the microbial fuel cell, the researchers designed a new electrode. They embedded iron and nickel oxides on a flexible carbon fiber cloth. When they heated the cloth in the presence of acetylene at 800°C, a forest of carbon nanofibers grew out of it. “The metal particles rode the growing fibers upward, so every fiber ended with a metal oxide tip,” the researchers say. So the electrode has conductive fibers with a catalytic tip. And bacteria cling to this rough conductive surface and form a thick film. The team used the same electrodes on both side of the fuel cell. When they ran sewage spiked with the antibiotic chloramphenicol through the cell, it removed 99.99% of the drug while producing hydrogen peroxide in two days. “Next, we plan to run it longer, test other drugs, check the toxicity of the breakdown products and link several cells in series to raise the power,” the team writes. “So can dirty water help pay for its own cleanup? Not completely yet. But in two days, our system turned sewage into cleaner water, a useful chemical and a little electricity.” Source : Yashmeen Budania et al. items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Protecting Forests from Disturbance Outperforms Restoration for Amazon Biodiversity, Study Finds Reading Time: 3 minutes Across 3 million hectares of the Brazilian Amazon, protecting forests from disturbance delivered greater biodiversity benefits than restoring already-cleared land, according to new research comparing conservation strategies. Conservation policy has long debated where limited funding should go: preventing deforestation outright, protecting standing forests from degradation, or restoring land already cleared. A study published in Science this September provides the clearest answer yet, using counterfactual scenarios built from observed land-use changes across three million hectares of the Brazilian Amazon’s deforestation frontier. Led by Leonardo S. Miranda of Lancaster University alongside researchers including Joice Ferreira of Embrapa, the team compared three intervention types against what actually happened on the ground. Protecting forests from disturbance, meaning avoiding fire and selective logging within standing forest, reduced biodiversity loss by 68.5% and carbon loss by 46.8% compared with the baseline scenario. Avoiding deforestation entirely mitigated 60.8% of carbon loss and 28.0% of biodiversity loss. Restoration of already-cleared land delivered the smallest gains for both outcomes. These findings challenge a common assumption in conservation funding, where restoration often receives outsized attention and investment despite standing forests requiring protection first. Protecting forests from disturbance proved nearly as effective as preventing deforestation for carbon storage, while substantially outperforming it for biodiversity outcomes, a distinction with direct implications for how governments and conservation organizations allocate resources. Neither single intervention alone reversed losses across the landscape. Combining avoided deforestation with protection from disturbance was necessary to achieve net-positive outcomes, increasing biodiversity by 12% and carbon by 18% above 2010 baseline levels. This combined approach proved essential precisely because deforestation and forest degradation operate through different mechanisms, requiring complementary rather than substitutable responses. Restoration still carries genuine value, particularly in landscapes where deforestation has already progressed extensively. The research team found that restoration delivered meaningful benefits, particularly on properties where much of the original forest cover had already disappeared, suggesting it works best as a complement to protection rather than a replacement. Protecting forests from disturbance addresses threats that often receive less policy attention than outright deforestation. Selective logging removes valuable timber species while leaving forest canopy nominally intact, and wildfires increasingly penetrate forest edges weakened by fragmentation and drought. Both processes degrade forest structure, reduce habitat quality for forest-dependent species, and release stored carbon, yet they generate far less public attention than visible clear-cutting. Protecting forests from disturbance targets fire and selective logging, threats that degrade forest structure without clear-cutting, with researchers finding that combined deforestation and disturbance avoidance are necessary to achieve net-positive biodiversity and carbon outcomes above 2010 baseline levels. Photo by Bill Salazar on Pexels. The study’s timing is especially urgent as climate change intensifies. The research team noted that combined interventions become increasingly important as warming progresses, since forest restoration efforts prove particularly vulnerable to wildfire risk. Newly planted or naturally regenerating young forests lack the structural resilience of mature canopies, making restoration investments vulnerable to being undone by the same fire disturbances the study identifies as critical to prevent. This vulnerability creates a policy challenge extending well beyond Brazil. As governments and international organizations increasingly emphasize forest restoration within climate commitments and biodiversity frameworks, protecting forests from disturbance offers a complementary message: restoration investments achieve far less impact when the remaining standing forest around them continues degrading from fire and logging. Joice Ferreira, principal investigator of the Capoeira restoration research program at Embrapa, emphasized that restoration remains essential precisely where forests have been lost across large areas, reinforcing that the study’s findings don’t diminish restoration’s role but rather clarify where and when it delivers the strongest returns. Restoration works best as part of integrated strategies rather than as a primary tool used independently of forest protection efforts. The research methodology itself offers a template for conservation planning elsewhere. By using observed land-use changes to construct counterfactual scenarios, the team measured what would have happened under different intervention choices and quantified trade-offs that previous studies could only estimate qualitatively. This approach allows policymakers to weigh cost-effectiveness directly rather than relying on intuition about which conservation strategy delivers the greatest return per dollar invested. As tropical deforestation frontiers worldwide face similar pressures from fire, logging, and agricultural expansion, protecting forests from disturbance provides an evidence-based framework extending beyond the Brazilian Amazon alone. The findings suggest that conservation funding achieves maximum impact not through any single strategy in isolation, but through carefully sequenced combinations addressing deforestation, degradation, and restoration simultaneously, each targeting the specific threats most relevant to a given landscape’s current condition. The post Protecting Forests from Disturbance Outperforms Restoration for Amazon Biodiversity, Study Finds appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: For centuries, the sacred groves of Rajasthan were understood as human gifts to nature -- places where belief drew a boundary and the forest was allowed to breathe. But as this essay quietly argues, the order of that story is wrong: people protected a handful of fig trees, and the birds did everything else. The peepal, the banyan, the gular -- three figs that tradition placed beyond the reach of the axe - fed birds through every lean season, and those birds, carrying seeds from across the landscape, built the grove outward from that protected center, generation after generation. "What belief really preserved was a process," the author writes, "a place where the planting could go on undisturbed for centuries." There is something worth sitting with in that realization: that the deepest acts of protection are often for something we cannot fully see, and that what looks like a tree standing alone is, if the birds still come, a forest in the making.

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Forest Landscape Restoration in Mozambique Launches in Nampula Province Reading Time: 3 minutes Forest landscape restoration in Mozambique has officially begun in Nampula Province, aiming to restore 500 hectares of Miombo woodland and build local livelihoods. Forest landscape restoration in Mozambique took a major step forward this August with the official launch of a new project in Nampula Province. The initiative pairs the Mozambican government with the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN), funded by Swiss Development Cooperation. Its goal is to turn national restoration pledges into work that communities can see on the ground. The launch unfolded over two days in Ribáuè District, starting with a briefing for provincial officials and continuing with a public ceremony. Government representatives, private companies, researchers, and local residents participated. Seedlings planted during the event were handed over to a nearby school, where students will track their growth. IUCN’s country representative in Mozambique described the project as reaching well beyond tree planting. The effort aims to improve land productivity and strengthen household livelihoods alongside ecological recovery. That framing positions forest landscape restoration in Mozambique as much an economic strategy as an environmental one. Over the next four years, the project will focus restoration work on 500 hectares within Ribáuè District. Of that total, 400 hectares will restore Miombo woodland, while the remaining 100 hectares will support agroforestry systems mixing crops with trees. The work contributes to Mozambique’s broader Five-Year Programme target of restoring 52,000 hectares nationwide. That national target also feeds into Mozambique’s international commitments under global restoration initiatives. Countries across Africa have pledged millions of hectares to these efforts over the past decade, though turning pledges into on-the-ground results has often proven difficult. A dedicated project with clear hectare targets and funding attached is meant to help close that gap. Miombo woodland stretches across a huge swath of south-central Africa, from Angola to Tanzania and across much of Mozambique. The ecosystem stores significant amounts of carbon and supports roughly half of Africa’s remaining elephant population. Millions of rural households also depend on it directly for firewood, food, and building materials. That dependence cuts both ways. Wood fuel accounts for a large share of household energy use across the Miombo region, which keeps pressure on the woodland high even where restoration work is underway. Providing communities with alternative income sources, rather than relying solely on wood and charcoal, is central to keeping any restored area intact over the long term. Alongside the restoration targets, the project will establish three plant nurseries to supply seedlings for ongoing work. Planners also intend to develop beekeeping and support sustainable value chains tied to cashew, bamboo, and legally harvested timber. Those activities aim to give residents income tied directly to keeping the landscape intact, a key piece of how forest landscape restoration in Mozambique is meant to work in practice. Forest landscape restoration in Mozambique ties livelihood directly to conservation, with three community nurseries, beekeeping, and sustainable value chains for cashew, bamboo, and timber giving Nampula residents concrete economic reasons to keep the landscape intact. Photo courtesy of IUCN . Mozambique’s project forms part of a larger global effort known as the FLR Hub, implemented by IUCN alongside other international partners. The hub originally supported restoration work across six countries in Africa and Latin America. A new contribution from Switzerland, announced in late 2025, extended that reach to Mozambique, bringing the total to seven participating countries. According to IUCN, the hub aims to shift restoration efforts from scattered, one-off projects to coordinated approaches that attract long-term investment. That shift matters for a landscape as large and fragmented as the Miombo, where piecemeal efforts have struggled to keep pace with ongoing degradation. Implementation in Ribáuè will rely on continued collaboration between government agencies, private businesses, universities, and civil society groups. Success will depend on whether restored land can deliver real income for residents, not just healthier soil and more trees. Four years is a short window to prove that the model works, but it gives the project a clear point at which results can be measured against the hectare targets set at launch. If it works, forest landscape restoration in Mozambique could offer a model other Miombo countries draw on as they pursue their own restoration commitments. The post Forest Landscape Restoration in Mozambique Launches in Nampula Province appeared first on Happy Eco News .

Τα εγκεκριμένα φάρμακα με την καλύτερη απόδοση για την πάθηση ξεπερνούν περίπου το 10,9%. Η θεραπεία, που ονομάζεται Μαγνητική e-Resonance Therapy (MeRT), αναπτύχθηκε από την Wave Neuroscience με έδρα την Καλιφόρνια σε συνεργασία με…
items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM A newly FDA-cleared treatment for PTSD reported 68 percent remission in clinical trials. The best-performing approved medications for the condition top out at around 10.9 percent. The treatment, called Magnetic e-Resonance Therapy (MeRT), was developed by California-based Wave Neuroscience in collaboration with researchers at the Texas A&M Health Institute of Biosciences and Technology. It pairs brain activity mapping with personalized magnetic stimulation. The clinical trial also reported a 52 percent reduction in PTSD symptoms overall. “Our FDA trial reported a 52 percent reduction in symptoms, so more than a four-fold increase in efficacy,” said Erik Won, D.O., Wave Neuroscience’s chief medical officer. “And more importantly, we saw 68 percent remission in our clinical trial. From a clinical care perspective, that’s really meaningful.” These results come from different studies, not a direct head-to-head comparison, but the gap is hard to ignore. How MeRT personalizes treatment The process starts with an electroencephalogram (EEG) that records each patient’s brain electrical activity. An AI-assisted algorithm uses that data to build a personalized stimulation plan. A coil placed against the scalp then delivers targeted magnetic pulses through transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS), a technique already FDA-cleared for treatment-resistant depression . Standard TMS follows a generalized protocol. MeRT adjusts based on what’s happening in each patient’s brain. Dr. Kenneth S. Ramos, a precision medicine researcher at Texas A&M Health who helped guide the study, put it this way: standard TMS covers the leak with a tarp; MeRT tries to find and replace the damaged shingles. Participants received five sessions per week over five to six weeks, but improvements appeared to persist after the sessions ended. The first FDA-cleared non-drug option for PTSD PTSD was formally recognized as a diagnosis in 1980 . Since then, treatment has relied on two FDA-approved medications, both SSRIs, and psychotherapy. A 2020 review found medication remission rates reached 10.9 percent at most. MeRT will be the first FDA-cleared non-medication treatment specifically for PTSD. Dr. Israel Liberzon, the study’s lead psychiatrist and a distinguished professor of psychiatry and behavioral sciences at the Texas A&M Naresh K. Vashisht College of Medicine, explained what that means for patients. “Right now, the FDA has approved only two medications for PTSD,” he said. “This is the first time that in addition to the medication, we have a non-medication option. There is psychotherapy that people use for PTSD, but psychotherapies require a lot of effort. People must participate actively, and many drop out because it’s too anxiety-provoking. So now we have a unique alternative.” About six percent of Americans will experience PTSD during their lifetime, with higher rates among women and veterans . In the United States, approximately 17.5 veterans die by suicide each day. “People living with PTSD have been left with trial-and-error treatment, medications and their side effects, and limited outcomes—even when treated by the most dedicated and experienced physicians,” Won said. “Wave’s FDA clearance signals a fundamentally different future: one in which PTSD can be objectively evaluated, precisely treated and meaningfully healed.” Wave Neuroscience and Texas A&M Health are working on insurance coverage to make the therapy more widely accessible. Won also believes MeRT could eventually be adapted for depression, anxiety, and other psychiatric conditions. Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary . items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Chances are, you’ve got a tube of toothpaste in your bathroom right now. If it’s only going on your teeth, you’re leaving a surprisingly useful cleaning tool sitting on your bathroom counter. Joy Ramos , a professional cleaner and operations manager at Bear Bros Cleaning, has long used toothpaste for jobs well beyond the bathroom. Most white, non-gel toothpastes contain mild abrasive particles that work like ultra-fine sandpaper, polishing surfaces without scratching them. It turns out that property has a lot of household uses. One thing before you start: plain white, non-gel toothpaste is what you want. Gel formulas don’t have the same abrasive particles, and heavily whitening varieties can be too harsh on delicate surfaces. Always rinse thoroughly after using it, and when in doubt, test on a discreet spot first. For scratches and cloudy surfaces A light scratch on glass (a phone screen, a coffee table, a mirror) can often be buffed out with a small amount of toothpaste on a microfiber cloth. Work in gentle circles, then wipe clean. The abrasives smooth the area around the scratch rather than filling it, so it becomes much less visible. The same trick works on fogged car headlights. Rub toothpaste over the lens in small circular motions for a minute or two, then rinse and dry. Repeat if needed. Wood is another one. Water rings and minor scratches on countertops or floors respond well to a small amount applied with a soft cloth. Follow the grain, wipe off, and dry thoroughly. For metals and fixtures Hard water takes the shine out of faucets and handles over time. Toothpaste can bring it back on stainless steel and chrome, though there’s a catch: softer metals like copper and brass can be damaged by the abrasives, so skip those. Silver jewelry is a great candidate, too. Avoid polished metals and soft stones like opals, pearls, or turquoise. “Always use a gentle hand and test first,” Ramos says. For walls, shoes, and more Crayon on painted walls is a classic small-kid problem. Toothpaste can lift it, but the wall finish matters. “Due to the mild abrasives in the paste, flat or matte paint may sometimes fade or become damaged,” Ramos says. “And on darker or more delicate finishes, it could leave dull spots or streaks.” Glossy, light-colored paint holds up well. Toothpaste also works on white rubber soles and leather or canvas sneakers. Just keep it away from suede, mesh, or anything delicate; those materials can stain or break down. For a persistent stain on a toilet seat, apply a small amount with a cloth or toothbrush, scrub gently, let it sit a few minutes, and wipe clean. Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary .
