items.descriptionOriginal: “Vibe coding,” is so last year. If you want to (try) to get on the same wavelength as teens and tweens, here’s another expression to add to your repertoire: Collins Dictionary has selected “mogging” as its 2026 word of the year. The slang term popular among Gen Z and Gen Alpha is defined as outperforming or outshining someone or something. Believed to be a shortened version of AMOG (alpha male of the group), the word traces back to bodybuilding culture around the 2010s. But it’s soared in popularity over the past year, with younger generations using it in a more playful way. Collins noted that experts found a 210% increase in usage of the “fast-growing slang word” in 2026, meriting the “word of the year” crown. So how do you use it? If your friend looks amazing in the selfie you just took, but your eyes are closed and hair is out of place — they’re mogging you. Or, to offer a more meta example, mogging is mogging the other words in the dictionary. Other words on the British dictionary’s shortlist include: Bixie : a haircut that’s shorter than a bob but longer than a pixie cut Fricy : a blend of fruity and spicy Friendslop : a low-budget, independently made video game designed to be played casually with friends Carspreading : the tendency of manufacturers to build cars that are longer, wider, and heavier Hydration break : a pause in a sporting contest to allow the contestants to drink fluids, especially in high heat Ghost job : a role advertised by an employer who has no intention of actually hiring anyone On Oct. 25, Dictionary.com announced its own word of the year: “Maxxing,” a shortened version of “maximizing” that can be used on its own or tacked on to the end of another word to describe the act of optimizing something. Derived from gamer lingo and in use for over a decade, the slang term broke through on TikTok in the 2020s. Its most famous usage is perhaps “looksmaxxing,” which refers to taking a person’s appearance to its full potential, but “sleepmaxxing,” “cozymaxxing,” and “booksmaxxing” have all joined the zeitgeist as well. “Really, anything in your life can get the maxxing treatment, if you do it wholeheartedly enough,” the online dictionary wrote in a blog post.

items.descriptionOriginal: P undits are describing last night as a romp for Democrats, a rebuke of Republicans, a blue tsunami, a rout in the red states. But underneath these headlines is a quieter, parallel story about voters choosing to abandon tribal allegiance and make decisions for themselves. For months, we’ve been hearing about the possibility of a blue wave — and then, in the same breath, the caveat: Is a wave even possible in today’s hyper-polarized America? And yet, in Texas, Florida, Kansas and beyond, the electorate refused to let party loyalty make their choice for them. Young, Latino and red-state voters moved, sometimes dramatically, in just two years. The composition of the two sides turned out to be less fixed than we imagined, with a meaningful number of voters willing to cast ballots across party lines when a candidate, issue or circumstance spoke to them. In Texas, where Democrats had historic wins, people of all parties have recently united to fight against a border wall through Big Bend National Park. Credit: Sam Karas Part of the story was turnout, said New York Times Chief Political Analyst Nate Cohn on The Daily . But, he added, “Many people who are registered as Republicans and voted for Donald Trump voted for the Democratic candidate.” This feels like a fitting conclusion to The Depolarization Project , our special series about how political polarization works and what we can do about it. The premise of that series was that depolarization isn’t about meeting in the middle. It’s about choosing to remain open and curious, rather than blindly clinging to arbitrary affiliations. In the end, many voters showed that their party label doesn’t have the final say. Data center opposition is proving to be a bipartisan, or even nonpartisan, issue across the U.S. Credit: Here Now / Shutterstock Wednesdays are normally “What We’re Reading” day here at Reasons to be Cheerful, so in that spirit, here’s a post-Election Day list of stories from our own depolarization series and from elsewhere around the web. We Hate to Break It to You, But Maybe We’re Not That Polarized – the New York Times A Wall Meant to Divide Is Uniting Left and Right in Texas – Reasons to be Cheerful Voters Vastly Underestimate the Open-Mindedness of Their Political Rivals – PsyPost The Door-to-Door Technique That Actually Changes Minds — Reasons to be Cheerful The post The Election That Transcended Tribalism appeared first on Reasons to be Cheerful .

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News The Walkable Traveler: Discovering Philadelphia’s Greenest Neighborhoods on Foot Reading Time: 3 minutes The Walkable Traveler: Discovering Philadelphia’s Greenest Neighborhoods on Foot There’s a moment on most city breaks when you realise you’ve spent more time getting between places than actually enjoying them. You’ve waited for a taxi, sat in traffic, arrived somewhere only to discover it’s a ten-minute walk from where you were half an hour ago. It’s enough to make you wonder why you bothered with the car in the first place. Philadelphia is a city where I’d be inclined to leave it behind.Not everywhere is within walking distance, obviously, but a surprising amount of the central area is. The streets are laid out in a fairly straightforward grid, and there’s plenty to see without travelling particularly far. I’d probably start somewhere around Independence Hall, partly because it’s one of those places you feel you ought to visit, and partly because the surrounding streets are worth a look in their own right. From there, Reading Terminal Market isn’t too far away. I wouldn’t bother making elaborate lunch plans. With that many food stalls under one roof, you’re almost certain to find something you fancy, although deciding what to eat might take longer than expected. Afterward, you could head towards Rittenhouse Square. I rather like the idea of a park that doesn’t try too hard to be an attraction. Rittenhouse is simply a pleasant place to sit for a while, with trees, benches and people going about their day. Somebody’s reading a book. Somebody else is walking a dog that clearly has no intention of going home yet. Meanwhile, the surrounding streets are full of shops, restaurants and apartments. It feels like a proper part of the neighbourhood rather than somewhere created exclusively for visitors. Philadelphia has quite a few green spaces like that, although some are much smaller. Community gardens are particularly interesting. You might find one occupying what was once an empty lot, with vegetables growing in raised beds and a few chairs tucked into a corner. They aren’t necessarily places you’d travel across the city to visit. But coming across one while walking through a residential neighbourhood is rather lovely. And they tell you something about the people who live there. I’d also make time for South Philadelphia. East Passyunk Avenue has the sort of mixture I enjoy: independent shops, restaurants, cafés and ordinary residential streets just around the corner. You can wander without feeling you’re missing some major attraction because you haven’t followed a particular route. The nearby Italian Market area is worth including too, especially if you like looking around food shops. I’d probably end up buying something completely impractical to carry around for the rest of the afternoon. One thing I wouldn’t do is try to squeeze all of Philadelphia into a single walking itinerary. It’s a sizeable city, and there’s no prize for finishing your holiday with sore feet. SEPTA’s buses, trolleys and trains make it possible to cover longer distances without needing a car, which is useful if you want to explore beyond the central neighbourhoods. Where you stay can make the whole thing easier or considerably more annoying. I once heard somebody describe a hotel as being ‘only twenty minutes from everything’, which sounds wonderful until you realise they meant twenty minutes by car. For a trip focused on walking, I’d be looking at the actual streets around the accommodation. Is there somewhere nearby for breakfast? Can you reach a park without crossing several major roads? How far is the nearest transit stop? Those details matter more to me than whether the apartment has an especially impressive television. One of the most effective ways to practice eco-friendly travel is reducing reliance on automobiles during city visits. Philadelphia’s grid layout makes it one of the most pedestrian- and transit-friendly cities in North America, allowing visitors to walk from historic landmarks to local farmers’ markets with ease. Choosing a neighborhood rental situated near public transportation hubs and neighborhood parks allows travelers to experience authentic community life while keeping emissions low. Rather than juggling multiple booking platforms, smart travelers use independent meta-search portals to find well-located accommodations. Exploring Philadelphia vacation rentals via cozycozy gives travelers real-time access to available townhomes, lofts, and historic suites across every major rental portal, making it effortless to lock in a sustainable home base. I’d check the final booking details separately, particularly the exact location and any additional charges. Of course, there’s an environmental benefit to doing more of a city break on foot. Fewer car journeys generally mean fewer transport emissions , and using public transport for longer trips can help reduce your reliance on taxis or a hire car. But I wouldn’t spend the whole weekend thinking about my carbon footprint.I’d be thinking about where to get another coffee, whether there’s time to explore one more street and why I hadn’t left myself longer at the market. That’s probably what makes walking such a good way to experience Philadelphia. You get to see the famous buildings, but you also spend time in the places between them. The little gardens, the corner shops, the streets where nothing especially remarkable is happening.And sometimes those are the bits you remember most. items.descriptionOriginal: As more of the planet’s wild places are consumed by human sprawl, people are increasingly trying to protect wildlife by moving it out of harm’s way. While such relocations might help a construction project clear a regulatory hurdle, it’s often not doing much good for the wildlife, according to new research. Just 6% of amphibian and reptile relocations tied to development could be classified as successful, according to a review of such projects published recently in Conservation Biology . “Moving these species away from a construction site does not mean they will survive in their new home,” said Megan Winand , a University of British Columbia biologist and the lead author. The results offer a sobering look at the performance of this increasingly popular strategy, as development of everything from pipelines to parks clashes with species protections. And while the authors found evidence of ways to improve the performance of such transplant projects, the main takeaway is that it’s usually better to avoid destroying a wild animal’s home than moving the creature to a new one. “We need to prioritize protecting habitat and explore alternatives to current mitigation practices, which this review shows are often failing to achieve meaningful conservation outcomes,” said Winand. The scale of the issue is staggering. While there is no comprehensive count of how often critters are moved to make way for development, a separate 2026 study by many of the same authors found that in British Columbia alone, some 5.1 million amphibians and reptiles were moved just between 2019 and 2022. And the long-term fate of these animals was unknown, because the province didn’t require monitoring. .IRPP_ruby , .IRPP_ruby .postImageUrl , .IRPP_ruby .centered-text-area {height: auto;position: transplanted animals fared. They scanned the scientific literature for papers published between 2007 and 2023 that examined the fate of relocated amphibians and reptiles. All told, they looked at 256 case studies tracking everything from tortoises to alligators. Most of the research was concentrated in North America, Europe, Australia and New Zealand. Nearly 70% of the translocations were done for conservation purposes, such as releasing an animal into habitat that it once occupied. The rest were cases involving animals moved to get them out of the way of development. The researchers then graded a relocation’s performance based on a four-tiered system. The first level was when the original transplants were surviving. A project reached level two when those survivors were reproducing. The third level came when the population was growing. The final, highest level was if a paper showed evidence that the population had achieved longterm viability. Based on that grading system, development-related relocations earned an abysmal grade. Just 6% of the cases were shown to have reached the third or fourth benchmarks. Nearly half of them failed to hit even the first level – that the original population had survived the move. While conservation-related transplants performed more than three times better, that still meant they only reached the top two levels 19% of the time. They had total failures in nearly a quarter of cases. A closer look at the different studies revealed two factors that seemed to contribute to the greater success of the conservation transplants, the scientists found. Things turned out better in cases where people tried to removed threats to an animal in the place where it was being relocated. Higher scores were also linked to more long-term monitoring after the move. “Without adequate follow-up, we won’t know whether animals survive in their new location, reproduce or establish a population that can survive over time,” says Winand. “Relocated animals may also leave the release sites, encounter new threats or face difficult habitat conditions.” So there are things people can do to increase the odds that the transplants will endure. The high failure rate of even the conservation-related measures shouldn’t be taken as a sign of poor execution by the people involved, the authors note. Rather, it illustrates how hard it is to do such translocations, especially for long-lived species that reproduce slowly. It also reinforces a common insight into biodiversity-related work: It’s a lot easier to avoid breaking something in the first place than to try to fix damage later. items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News How Vietnamese Farmers Built a Rice Straw Circular Economy that Pays Reading Time: 3 minutes A rice straw circular economy in Vietnam’s Mekong Delta turns leftover stalks into mushrooms and compost. Rice straw circular economy models give Vietnamese farmers a reason to stop burning their fields. At New Green Farm Cooperative in the Mekong Delta, leftover stalks now feed mushroom beds and compost piles. As a result, member farmers have cut their use of chemical nitrogen fertilizer by 40%. The cooperative works with about 100 farming households across 148 hectares. In its operating area, straw burning has dropped by 90-95%. Farmers are earning more while their fields send up far less smoke. Burning has long been the default after harvest. It clears fields quickly and costs nothing up front. It also fills the air with smoke and dust and releases planet-warming gases. A circular economy offers another path. It keeps materials in use, so one process’s waste becomes the next one’s raw material. In a rice straw circular economy, the stalks become food, fertilizer, and income. New Green Farm put this idea to work in 2023, starting with seven core members. Director Dong Van Canh partnered with the International Rice Research Institute (IRRI) through the RiceEco project. The Mekong-Republic of Korea Cooperation Fund pays for RiceEco, which supports Vietnam’s One Million Hectares program for low-emission rice. After harvest, a local machinery company bales the straw with mechanized equipment. The cooperative grows mushrooms on about 9,000 bales a year, or roughly 25 a day. Straw also goes into compost, which returns nutrients to the rice fields. That compost explains the drop in chemical fertilizer. Using less fertilizer saves farmers USD 57 to 65 per hectare each season. Selling their straw adds another USD 13 to 15 per hectare per crop. For the cooperative, each mushroom bale earns about 38 US cents in profit, or roughly USD 3,400 a year. Compost adds about USD 2,700 a year, or USD 38 per ton for 72 tons. Canh says the model gives farmers more than one way to earn. Rice still brings in about 60% of the cooperative’s income, while mushrooms add about 30%. Compost, vegetables, and other products make up the rest. In a rice straw circular economy, farmers grow more than rice and cultivate new income sources. Rice provides about 60% of the cooperative’s earnings, while mushrooms contribute another 30%, with compost, vegetables, and other products filling out the rest. Photo by Petr Ganaj on Pexels. That income mix has helped the business grow. Operating space has expanded from 2,500 to about 11,000 square meters, roughly two American football fields. Products now reach buyers in Ho Chi Minh City and on Phu Quoc Island. Canh’s role has changed over time. He moved from field labor to organizing production, managing staff, and finding buyers. His wife runs the cooperative’s onion and chili pepper plots. Other cooperatives in the delta are seeing similar results. In Can Tho, the Tien Thuan Agricultural and Service Cooperative received straw balers and composting machines in June 2024. By September 2025, it was producing 12 to 15 tons of organic fertilizer a month. Circular methods there add USD 50 to 70 of value per hectare. Burning straw or selling it loose adds only about USD 25. The cooperative’s mushroom houses produce up to 1,050 kilograms every six weeks. Farmers there report that field crabs and earthworms have returned, both signs of healthier soil. The work has also created new jobs, especially for women. Machines now handle much of the heavy labor of clearing fields. An estimated 30 to 40% of nearby farmers have adopted similar methods. That uptake matters, because a rice straw circular economy depends on many farms supplying straw. The approach also works outside the delta. In northern Ninh Binh Province, the Nam Cuong cooperative composts rice straw with cow manure for its potatoes. A mechanized turner has cut composting time from 90 days to 45. Potato fields that received this compost yielded 19 to 28 tons per hectare. Plots without it needed 20% more potassium and nitrogen fertilizer. The cooperative now supplies organic produce to meal programs at 20 local schools. Growth has exposed some weak points. New Green Farm faces cash-flow gaps between harvests and limited capital to expand. Storage space also runs short during peak seasons. Affordable loans and better baling equipment would help close those gaps. The cooperative plans larger warehouses for straw collection. Project partners also aim to bring the model to other cooperatives. RiceEco has already brought the rice straw circular economy to 5,084 farmers and other stakeholders. It supports four pilot businesses in Vietnam and Cambodia. Its work also informed Vietnam’s 2023 national guideline on sustainable rice straw management. For generations, people saw straw as something to get rid of. Cooperatives like New Green Farm have turned it into mushrooms, compost, and steady income. The rice straw circular economy shows that the answer to field burning can also be a business plan. The post How Vietnamese Farmers Built a Rice Straw Circular Economy that Pays appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News From Climate Disasters to Resilient Cities: Connecting Technology, Nature, and Communities Reading Time: 3 minutes From Texas floods to Himalayan glacier collapse, cities built for a climate that no longer exists are discovering that real resilience means connecting technology, nature, and people, not just adding more sensors. Before dawn on July 4, 2025, the Guadalupe River at Kerrville rose from about 3 feet to 30 feet in just 45 minutes, turning part of the Texas Hill Country into a disaster zone. In August 2026, a glacier collapse near the Nepal-Tibet border triggered catastrophic flooding that damaged settlements, roads and hydropower infrastructure. Toronto and Southern Ontario have faced their own warning signs. In July 2024, intense rainfall flooded highways and subway stations, while a major power outage affected nearly 300,000 customers. Canada’s 2026 wildfire season has also forced evacuations. These events are geographically different, but they expose a common vulnerability: many cities were built for a climate that no longer exists. Infrastructure designed around historical weather conditions is increasingly being tested by more intense rainfall, extreme heat, wildfires and other climate hazards. We are also pushing against planetary limits. The pressure is broader than climate change alone. The 2025 Planetary Health Check found that seven of the nine planetary boundaries have been crossed, including climate change, freshwater change, biosphere integrity, and ocean acidification. These pressures interact. Damage to ecosystems can weaken carbon sinks, while climate change can disrupt freshwater cycles. In 2026, the United Nations University warned of “global water bankruptcy,” describing water systems so depleted or degraded that they may no longer easily return to historical conditions. For cities, these pressures quickly become infrastructure challenges. Extreme rainfall overwhelms stormwater systems. Heat stresses buildings, electricity grids and public health. Drought and groundwater depletion threaten water security. This is why mitigation and adaptation cannot be treated as separate agendas. Mitigation reduces the emissions driving future warming. Adaptation reduces impacts that are already occurring or can no longer be fully avoided. Yet adaptation has a major financing problem. UNEP estimates that developing countries will need about US$310 billion to US$365 billion annually by 2035, while international public adaptation finance flows were only US$26 billion in 2023. Adaptation needs are now roughly 12 to 14 times current flows. Resilience plans cannot remain on paper when cities need drainage, cooling, early-warning and water systems now. What does a climate-resilient city actually look like? Smart buildings can reduce energy demand through efficient design, sensors and automated controls while improving thermal comfort and indoor air quality. At the neighbourhood scale, renewables, storage, microgrids and electric mobility can reduce emissions while strengthening resilience. Internet of Things, or IoT, technologies can monitor rainfall, drainage, temperature and infrastructure performance. But a community is not “smart” simply because it has more sensors. Some of the most powerful solutions work with natural systems. Low-impact development and sustainable stormwater management use rain gardens, bioswales, permeable pavements, green roofs, infiltration areas, and rainwater harvesting to retain, absorb, filter, or reuse rainfall close to where it falls. Blue-green infrastructure extends this through wetlands, urban forests, ponds, and waterways. The principle is simple: instead of designing cities only to move water away as quickly as possible, we can design them to absorb, store, filter, and reuse it. Blue-green infrastructure shifts urban water management from moving rainfall away as fast as possible to absorbing, storing, filtering, and reusing it through rain gardens, bioswales, wetlands, green roofs, and urban forests built into the city fabric. Photo by Shox Art on Pexels. Bangladesh offers a powerful community-level example. In salinity-affected coastal areas, women trained as “Pani Apas,” or water sisters, help households use and maintain rainwater-harvesting systems. The model does more than provide water tanks. It connects climate adaptation with safer water, women’s livelihoods, skills and community ownership. UNDP reports that related coastal initiatives provide year-round safe drinking water to nearly 140,000 people in parts of Khulna and Satkhira. Costa Rica offers a different lesson from Latin America. Since 2015, nearly all of its electricity has come from renewable sources, with hydropower supplying around 70%, alongside wind and geothermal power. Yet prolonged dry periods increasingly challenge hydropower production. Costa Rica therefore illustrates why mitigation and adaptation must advance together. A clean electricity system still needs diversified renewables, resilient grids and water-aware planning. The five Ps of sustainable development, People, Planet, Prosperity, Peace, and Partnership, provide a useful way to judge these solutions. People ask who is protected. Planet asks whether emissions, water, and ecosystems are considered together. Prosperity asks whether investment creates livelihoods and resilient infrastructure. Peace brings in fairness, trust and accountable institutions. Partnership recognizes that governments, communities, engineers, businesses and civil society organizations must work together. The major gap today is often not the absence of solutions. It is our failure to connect them, finance them adequately, implement them equitably and maintain them over time. Sensors can warn us that water is rising. Blue-green infrastructure can help absorb it. Rainwater harvesting can turn rainfall into a resource. Clean electricity can reduce emissions. But people still need the knowledge, resources and authority to operate these systems and shape the decisions behind them. A truly smart and resilient city is not the one with the most connected devices. It is the one that connects technology, nature, infrastructure and people well enough to reduce risk before disaster occurs, protect the most vulnerable and recover more equitably when disruption cannot be avoided. The post From Climate Disasters to Resilient Cities: Connecting Technology, Nature, and Communities appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.title: 28 Χρόνια Περπάτημα, Μια Μητέρα Πόρτα
items.titleOriginal: 28 Years Walking, One Mother's Doorstep
items.description: Ο Karl Bushby έφυγε από τη Χιλή με τα πόδια το 1998 σε ηλικία 29 ετών, με χρυσά μαλλιά και δύο σιδερένιους κανόνες: χωρίς μηχανές να τον μεταφέρουν μπροστά και χωρίς να γυρίζει σπίτι — ούτε για ασθένεια, ούτε για θλίψη, ούτε για τίποτα. Είκοσι οκτώ χρόνια, 75 εκατομμύρια βήματα, μια συνάντηση με πολική αρκούδα, 31 ημέρες κολύμπι στην Κασπία Θάλασσα και ένα κελί φυλακής στον Παναμά αργότερα, πήγε στη μητέρα του».…
items.descriptionOriginal: Karl Bushby left Chile on foot in 1998 at age 29, with golden hair and two iron rules: no machines to carry him forward, and no coming home — not for illness, not for grief, not for anything. Twenty-eight years, 75 million steps, one polar bear encounter, 31 days swimming the Caspian Sea, and a jail cell in Panama later, he walked up to his mother's house in Hull, England, pushing the same cart he'd had for a quarter century. The cheers fell quiet at the doorstep. What lingers most isn't the staggering mileage but the strange disorientation of arrival — he found himself looking the wrong way crossing the road in his own country, a foreigner in his birthplace. "I'm home, but it's not the home that I'm used to now for so long," he said. "I almost feel guilt." Nearly half his life spent walking the earth had multiplied his sense of belonging until home meant something far larger and more complicated than a red-brick terrace in northern England. His parting thought wasn't about endurance or willpower — it was a quiet insistence that the world is full of people who have drastically underestimated themselves, and that the first step is simply imagining otherwise.

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Upcycling Food Industry Byproducts into Ingredients People Want to Eat Reading Time: 3 minutes Upcycling food industry byproducts turns factory leftovers into tasty, useful ingredients. Dutch company Greencovery shows how this can work for food makers. Upcycling food industry byproducts means turning leftover material from food factories into new ingredients. Food makers often call these leftovers side streams. Many side streams end up discarded or sold as animal feed. Greencovery , a company based in Wageningen in the Netherlands, wants to change that. It says its patented technology recovers valuable ingredients from side streams. The goal is to create new revenue for manufacturers and a lighter footprint on the planet. The scale of food waste is large. The UN Environment Programme reported that the world wasted 1.05 billion metric tons of food in 2022. That equals about 19% of the food available to consumers. Those figures cover homes, restaurants, and stores, not factory leftovers. Still, they show why finding new uses for food matters. Food loss and waste also affect the climate. The same report links it to 8% to 10% of global greenhouse gas emissions. That is almost five times the emissions from the aviation sector. A side stream is the material left after a factory makes its main product. That material often still holds useful compounds. Greencovery focuses on pulling those compounds out and returning them to the food supply. Animal feed is a common destination for these leftovers. Greencovery describes it as a lower-value outcome than human food. Its team sees upcycling food industry byproducts as a way to move more material toward food ingredients. The company uses what it calls mild separation technology. Separation means pulling the useful parts out of a mixture. Mild means gentle conditions, and the company says the method uses less energy and water than other separation techniques. Why does that matter? The company says the ingredients it extracts carry a low carbon footprint. A carbon footprint measures the greenhouse gases released to make a product. The recovered ingredients bring three listed strengths: high functionality, great taste, and microbial stability. Functionality means an ingredient performs well in recipes. Microbial stability means it resists spoilage by microbes and holds up in storage. Upcycling food industry byproducts turns okara, the often-overlooked soy pulp left after soy milk or tofu production, into Okara Pro and Okara Tex, two neutral-tasting, nutritious ingredients suited to bakery goods, savory dishes, and plant-based meat. Photo by Polina Tankilevitch on Pexels. Greencovery does not stop at the lab. It guides partners through three checkpoints for upcycling food industry byproducts. Each one answers a question. Does it work? Does the market want it? Is it commercially viable? The first checkpoint is a proof of concept, which tests whether the idea works technically. The team also runs early product trials to see if a side stream can become a functional ingredient. Next comes a proof of market, which checks whether buyers want the product. The team tests taste, function, and nutrition. It also brings potential buyers into the conversation early. The final step is a proof of business. It covers pricing, costs, profit margins, and supply chains. Greencovery also co-invests with partners and helps set up production in a suitable location. The team blends technology experts, food application specialists, and business experts. Together, they test both the science and the numbers. Two real products show upcycling food industry byproducts at work. The company has made a high-fiber satay sauce and a Parmigiano Reggiano mayonnaise. Both reflect its aim of using ingredients that might otherwise be discarded. The Dutch Prime Minister met the team and experienced both products firsthand. The meeting took place during the Netherlands’ food waste awareness week. Foodvalley NL, a group that promotes innovation and sustainability in food, invited Greencovery to the event. The talks focused on cutting food waste and finding better uses for ingredients. Greencovery also thanked the Upcycling Community for its support. Greencovery says it works to speed up the path from idea to market. Faster launches help companies see returns sooner. Manufacturers curious about their own side streams can start small. Greencovery offers a free 30-minute consultation call. These claims come from Greencovery itself, so readers should treat them as company-reported. Food makers considering upcycling their food byproducts should run their own trials and check local food safety rules before launching a product. Shoppers can play a part too. Choosing upcycled foods signals demand, which encourages more companies to try. Shoppers interested in upcycling food industry byproducts should read labels closely. A product can earn the upcycled label with only 10% upcycled ingredients by weight, so it helps to learn what the upcycled label actually requires. Organic foods, by comparison, must contain at least 95% certified organic ingredients. Food waste remains a large problem, but practical tools to shrink it are taking shape. Upcycling food industry byproducts gives manufacturers a clear path from leftover to ingredient. With testing, market checks, and careful planning, a side stream can become a product people choose to buy. The post Upcycling Food Industry Byproducts into Ingredients People Want to Eat appeared first on Happy Eco News .

Ο λόγος της ήταν απλός. «Δεν θα συμμετείχε σε AC…
items.descriptionOriginal: This article is part of The Optimist Daily’s Local Changemakers 2026 series, spotlighting changemakers 30 and under. Earlier this year, on a trip to Dominica to learn about the sperm whales that live in those Caribbean waters, Maya Higa was offered the chance to swim with them. She said no. Her reason was simple. “She would not participate in an activity that her followers would not be able to do,” wrote Maggie Kaplan, who nominated Maya for this series and was on the same trip. For most wildlife creators, that would have been the perfect moment for the cameras to come out. Maya turned on her livestream instead, talked with the boat crew and local staff about their work and lives, and shared the whales from her view on the surface. Kaplan came away moved by Maya’s resolve. “I was very impressed with her dedication on all fronts,” she wrote. But what she was describing wasn’t a sacrifice. It was consistency. Maya was doing exactly what she built Alveus Sanctuary to do. Building Alveus Maya founded Alveus in 2021 with a 21-hour charity stream on Twitch that raised more than $500,000. The platform came after the expertise, not the other way around. She grew up in Northern California and studied agricultural education and communication at Cal Poly San Luis Obispo. In college, she took a job as a zookeeper and completed internships at AZA-accredited facilities. She even got her falconry license. Part of the work involved going to schools and birthday parties to teach kids about animals in person, which gave her a taste for hands-on outreach and education. She went on to become a licensed wildlife rehabilitator. When she started streaming, all of that prior knowledge and experience came with her. What exactly is Alveus? Alveus is both a physical wildlife sanctuary in Austin, Texas, and a virtual education center. The sanctuary houses non-releasable animal ambassadors, which are animals that can’t survive in the wild but can represent their species and the ecosystems they come from. A 24/7 livestream on Twitch lets viewers watch them, get to know them by name, and connect with information about their wild counterparts. Other content creators can visit the sanctuary, run education programs, and extend the conservation message into communities Alveus wouldn’t otherwise reach. Conservation for a generation that grew up on Twitch The demographic Maya is reaching is one that traditional conservation organizations have struggled with for years. Maya “is reaching a whole new generation of 18 to 30 year olds through social media platforms that speak to their demographic,” Kaplan wrote. That generation didn’t grow up watching nature documentaries on television. They watch streams, follow creators, and decide what they care about based on communities they already belong to. “She is creating a new type of outreach,” Kaplan wrote, “a teaching platform about different species and their importance to our environment.” A teaching platform built around the creator-viewer relationship works differently from a broadcast. Viewers are compelled to come back. They recognize the individual animals. They get into discussions in the chat about things they’ve learned. Conservation education needs that kind of sustained attention, and with conventional methods, it doesn’t get it very often. Maya has over a million followers across her platforms, and those followers have made Alveus financially self-sustaining through their donations. Twitch donated $100,000 to the sanctuary directly. A partnership with WWF extended the work beyond the sanctuary itself. And Maya’s own TED talk, “ The wildlife sanctuary you can visit from anywhere ,” which she delivered in Vancouver, Canada, earlier this year, brought the model to an even broader professional audience. What comes next By 2026, Alveus has raised more than $7.5 million for conservation causes since its founding. The organization is actively expanding: new animal ambassadors coming in, enclosures being built out, and staff added to keep pace. Two projects are currently underway. The Pollinator Census is Alveus’s first community science initiative, where community members observe pollinator species in the sanctuary’s garden, and entomologists identify them, generating data to support insect conservation research. The greater effort is the Alveus Research and Recovery Institute (ARRI), developed in partnership with the Association of Zoos and Aquariums ‘ Saving Animals from Extinction (SAFE) program. ARRI’s first goal is a conservation breeding and release program for two critically endangered species: the Mexican Gray wolf and the Red wolf. It moves Alveus from education into direct intervention in species survival. The sperm whale moment in Dominica illustrates something about the whole operation. Maya went to Dominica to learn. When the choice came up, she ran the same calculation she’s always run: the point isn’t the experience she gets to have. It’s the one her audience gets to share with her. With a million people watching, that adds up to a different kind of reach than the field has seen. Learn more at bio.link/mayahiga . The post Maya Higa built a wildlife sanctuary on Twitch, funded by the people who watch it first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News .

items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Two coral fragments fell over in a Stanford lab tank. When they touched, one healed the other. The bleached fragment, starved of the symbiotic algae that give coral both its color and its nutrition, began recovering within days. “We watched the healthy coral send over these colourful beneficial algae over to the bleached corals, and we watched its colour restore basically in front of our eyes,” said ocean scientist Danny Collins . Within a couple of weeks, the dying coral had recovered to the point where it was indistinguishable from its healthy neighbor. “We were blown away,” Collins said. “It does seem like this could open a door to possible reef restoration.” The findings , published last month in Science Advances , suggest that bleached coral is not necessarily dead, and that it can recover faster than researchers expected. The magic of the tissue bridge The recovery requires direct physical contact and a genetic match. When Collins’s team separated the fragments by a few millimeters, nothing happened. When they introduced corals from different genetic backgrounds, the corals rejected each other the way a body might reject a donated organ. When genetic clones made contact, their tissues fused. “They create a tissue bridge that kind of acts as a nutrient highway that allows for the healthy coral to then send over nutrients and this colourful algae over to the bleached coral,” Collins said. Coral is a colonial animal, a single organism made of thousands to millions of individual polyps. Fragments of the same genetic background recognize each other on contact and merge rather than fight. Collins noted this serves a natural function. If a piece breaks off in a wave, it can reconnect with the original colony. 96 percent of reefs are at risk The International Union for Conservation of Nature announced that about 96 percent of the world’s shallow-water reef systems are critically endangered and could disappear by 2075. Coral reefs support between a quarter and a third of all marine species, along with fisheries and coastal economies that hundreds of millions of people depend on. Coral scientist Julia Cole, who was not involved in the study, called the Stanford findings “a glimmer of light.” Cole chairs the Department of Earth and Environmental Sciences at the University of Michigan. She was enthusiastic but clear-eyed about scale. “If you think about the scale of reefs as kilometers, or in the case of the biggest reefs, thousands of kilometers … something that requires coral-to-coral contact, it would be a very meticulous and kind of overwhelming project,” she said. Collins’s team is working on extracting algae from healthy reefs, culturing it in labs, and deploying it to protect at-risk reefs ahead of expected bleaching events. “We hope in the near future we can have some interventions that actually could be field deployable and possibly scalable,” he said. The restoration work doesn’t address what’s warming the ocean in the first place. “We know how to solve the warming climate that’s causing these problems,” Cole said. “It comes back to getting serious about reducing greenhouse gas emissions, getting off of fossil fuels and transitioning to a clean-energy economy .” Source study: Science Advances – Rapid coral bleaching recovery via symbiont transfer from healthy corals Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary . items.descriptionOriginal: Dietary guidelines seem to run the gamut depending on where you live. In Japan, grain-based dishes are the main focus, while Greece promotes the Mediterranean diet and the U.S. emphasizes protein . So nutrition scientists from around the globe recently came together to develop a compendium of advice that’s adaptable across cultures (and takes the health of the planet into account). Enter: the International Food Guide Pyramid. The team compared national and regional dietary guidelines from the United States, Canada, Germany, Australia, China, the Netherlands, and the Nordic countries, in addition to analyzing more than 250 scientific publications, to pinpoint the shared fundamentals of healthy eating. As it turns out, they may be more universal than it often seems. “Despite what people often hear, there’s actually substantial agreement in nutrition science about the foundations of healthy eating,” study lead Karen Della Corte said in a news release. She added that a balanced diet will look different for each person, so the guidelines are designed to be adjusted to include local, affordable, and culturally appropriate foods. The new food pyramid focuses on plant foods, healthier sources of fat and protein, and high-quality carbohydrates. At the base — representing the foundation of a nourishing diet — are vegetables and fruit as well as whole and low-glycemic index grains. Above that are plant-based proteins like beans, nuts, and seeds, as well as plant-based oils. Next up are fish, poultry, eggs, and certain dairy products, and at the top, for use sparingly, are refined grains, red and processed meats, butter, chips, sugary drinks and snacks, and salt. A 2025 report from the EAT-Lancet commission called for similarly plant-forward international guidelines, suggesting they could prevent 15 million premature deaths per year and reduce environmental impacts like greenhouse gas emissions. “Our diet has to be not only for our own health but also for the health of our planet,” said David Jenkins of the University of Toronto, creator of the glycemic index. “Our science base has to be appropriately comprehensive to include that.” Karen Della Corte Corte offered the following advice for putting the pyramid’s principles into practice: Design your meal around the plant food you want to emphasize, first thinking about which vegetables, whole grains, beans, or lentils you could include. Opt for beans, peas, lentils, fish, poultry, or yogurt more frequently than red or processed meats, and don’t make meat the biggest part of any meal. Reach for snacks like nuts, seeds, fruit, or vegetables with hummus over less nutritious processed options. Choose whole-grain bread over refined white bread and whole-grain or high-fiber cereals rather than refined, puffed, flaked, or popped cereals. Use canola or olive oil in your cooking instead of animal fats like butter or tallow. Drink water instead of soda.

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Endangered Animals Making a Comeback in 2027 Reading Time: 4 minutes Endangered Animals Making a Comeback in 2027 When you hear about endangered wildlife, it’s often another story of shrinking habitats, declining populations or species facing extinction. However, there is good news worth celebrating, too. Thanks to dedicated conservation efforts, some of the world’s most threatened animals are making remarkable comebacks. From mountain gorillas thriving in protected forests to bald eagles soaring across North America, you’ll find encouraging examples of how conservation can reverse population declines. Discover inspiring wildlife recovery stories that offer hope to endangered animals and show how your support for conservation can make a difference. 1. Mountain Gorillas Decades of habitat protection, veterinary care and anti-poaching initiatives have helped mountain gorilla populations grow to over 1,000 individuals , with multiple family groups. It’s a significant improvement for a species that once faced a much bleaker future. You’ll find these great apes in two isolated regions of Central and East Africa, where conservation teams work alongside local communities to protect the remaining habitat. The survival of this primate species extends beyond the gorillas themselves. Protecting large primates can also preserve entire ecosystems. While mountain gorillas remain endangered, their growing numbers demonstrate the value of long-term conservation. Expanding these efforts to other primate species may also protect smaller endangered species. 2. Bald Eagles Few wildlife recoveries are as impressive as that of the bald eagle. Once threatened by hunting, habitat destruction and the irresponsible use of the pesticide commonly known as DDT, America’s national bird has made an extraordinary species comeback. DDT led to poor-quality egg production, making successful breeding incredibly difficult for bald eagles. The ban on DDT, stronger legal protections and habitat conservation helped reverse decades of population decline. According to the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, the population in the lower 48 states increased from approximately 72,434 birds in 2009 to just over 316,000 birds , with 71,467 breeding pairs tracked between 2018 and 2019. Today, you’ll see bald eagles near rivers, lakes and coastlines across much of North America. Their remarkable recovery shows how environmental laws and sustained conservation efforts can give threatened wildlife a second chance. 3. Sea Turtles For sea turtles, the journey to adulthood begins with a dangerous dash from nest to ocean. Fortunately, conservation programs are giving more hatchlings a fighting chance through beach patrols, nest monitoring and community involvement. In the Philippines, conservationists have even recruited four-legged helpers. Project CURMA’s Paw Patrol uses specially trained dogs to sniff out buried turtle eggs , allowing volunteers to locate and protect nests from poachers and other threats. Efforts to reduce accidental catches in fishing nets, restore nesting beaches and limit artificial lighting along the coastlines are helping protect sea turtles at different stages of their lives. Some populations have shown encouraging improvements following decades of protection. While several sea turtle species remain endangered or critically endangered, initiatives like these show that creative conservation strategies can improve their chances of survival. When you participate in community initiatives, such as Paw Patrol, you increase the support that struggling species need to survive. 4. Tigers Tigers have lost much of their historical range to deforestation, human development and poaching. However, conservation efforts in parts of Asia are helping these magnificent predators reclaim lost ground. Wild tigers live across parts of Asia, where conservation efforts have helped some populations rebound after the global population fell to an estimated 3,200 in 2010. India offers one of the strongest examples, as it is now home to about 70% of the world’s wild tigers. Forest conservation has played a valuable part in this and other success stories. Sustainable forestry and other interventions have slowed global deforestation rates by almost 40% since the 1990s, which is why purchasing sustainably sourced timber is so important, whether you buy new floors, furniture or even musical instruments. Habitat loss remains a threat, but support for responsible forest management offers hope. 5. American Alligators American alligators were once hunted so extensively for their valuable skins that their survival became a serious concern. By 1967, the species had gained federal endangered status, prompting stronger protections against hunting and illegal trade. Conservation measures, including regulated harvesting and wetland management, helped restore their numbers. The species was removed from the U.S. endangered species list in 1987, just two decades after receiving protection. Today, up to 1.06 million mature American alligators inhabit the southeastern United States. With the species now classified as least concern, you’re looking at one of America’s most successful wildlife recovery stories. 6. Other Stories of Recovery The good news continues across the world. Other threatened species are showing encouraging signs of recovery, giving you even more reasons to feel hopeful about wildlife conservation. The Iberian lynx has rebounded from near extinction, thanks to captive breeding and habitat restoration across Spain and Portugal. North Atlantic right whales are also showing tentative signs of population growth, although their survival remains precarious. Meanwhile, giant pandas have benefited from decades of habitat protection and breeding programs, while southern white rhinos have recovered significantly from historical population lows through intensive conservation efforts. Humpback whales offer another success story, with several populations rebounding after commercial whaling restrictions gave these ocean giants a chance to recover. These achievements highlight the importance of patience and persistence, as rebuilding wildlife populations often requires decades of protection and ongoing monitoring. Every contribution makes a difference, and even keeping your distance from these animals, respecting protected habitats and choosing ethical wildlife tourism experiences contribute to various species’ success stories. Why Are More Endangered Animals Recovering? Wildlife recovery rarely happens by chance. Behind these success stories are years of coordinated conservation efforts, scientific research and communities working to protect vulnerable species. These efforts also benefit entire ecosystems. When you protect forests, wetlands and oceans, you’re helping preserve the habitats that countless species depend on for survival. Several approaches are helping endangered animals rebuild their populations: Habitat protection: National parks, wildlife corridors and sustainable land management give animals safer places to live, breed and find food. Stronger wildlife laws: Hunting restrictions, anti-poaching patrols and international trade regulations help reduce human-driven threats. Breeding and reintroduction programs: Conservationists can raise threatened animals in protected environments and then release them into suitable habitats where they have a better chance of thriving. Community involvement: Local conservation projects encourage people to protect wildlife while supporting livelihoods through responsible tourism and sustainable practices. Scientific monitoring: Tools like GPS collars, population surveys, and genetic research help conservationists spot problems earlier and celebrate progress when recovery efforts work. A Brighter Future for Endangered Wildlife Every species making a comeback represents years of dedication and a reminder that extinction isn’t always inevitable. Although many endangered animals still face serious threats, these conservation successes show that meaningful progress is possible. You can help sustain that momentum by supporting wildlife conservation organizations, choosing responsibly sourced products and spreading awareness about threatened species. Even small actions contribute to a broader movement to protect biodiversity. With continued commitment, today’s recovery stories could become tomorrow’s thriving wildlife populations. The post Endangered Animals Making a Comeback in 2027 appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: A former Los Angeles gang member, a former skinhead and a former radical Islamist walk into a youth center. What sounds like the setup for an uneasy joke is at the core of Farah Pandith’s work: Put people who might otherwise never share a room in front of young people; let them explain what drew them into extremism and how they found their way out. “They’re the most authentic and credible voices there are,” Pandith says. More than once she has observed that their stories reach an audience that official warnings cannot. For decades, including while working for the U.S. government under the Obama, George W. Bush and George H.W. Bush administrations, Pandith researched why people embrace ideologies that divide the world into “us versus them.” Before people can be persuaded away from hatred, she argues, one has to understand what they are looking for: recognition, certainty or a place in the world. “You don’t suddenly explode and become an extremist overnight. You’re having some self-doubt, you’re asking questions about who you are,” she says from her light-filled living room in Arlington, Virginia. Preventing someone from becoming an extremist has been her lifelong goal, because it’s “infinitely easier than dealing with the fallout.” Farah Pandith visits the Indonesian city of Bekasi during her time as the U.S. special representative to Muslim communities. Credit: U.S. Embassy, Jakarta / Wikimedia Commons While working for the government, she traveled to nearly 100 countries, from Belgium to Bangladesh, to understand how extremists’ descent into violence can be interrupted. Today she applies what she learned to a broader problem: how to make compassion more than an admirable sentiment and help communities put it into practice. Last year Pandith received the ADL Daniel Pearl Award , which is given annually to a person who has had a positive impact on understanding between Jews and the Muslim world, and is sponsored by the parents of the journalist who was kidnapped and killed in Pakistan in 2002. “It is hard to think of anyone more knowledgeable than Farah Pandith when it comes to countering violent extremism,” Joseph Nye, the late chair of the National Intelligence Council, said about her. On September 11, 2001, Pandith watched on television like millions of others as two planes struck the World Trade Center. “It felt very heavy,” she recalls, putting a hand to her heart. “The world kind of went still for a moment, like, ‘What do we do about this?’” She felt compelled to act, to help prevent such violence from happening again. She especially rejected the way extremists attempted to define her religion on the airwaves. “Who are they to dictate what Islam is?” she remembers thinking. “For me, Islam means humility, compassion, to treat others with respect.” Initially, when she worked for the U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID), cooperating with local organizations showed her that effective policy depends on understanding the people on the ground. “You have to listen really well to find a solution that matches with the local community,” she says. “That’s tricky and complex. Trust has to be built first.” The same principle, she realized, applied to preventing violent extremism. Government officials could not design effective strategies from Washington alone. They needed to hear from the people they hoped to reach, including those whose voices had been overlooked. After joining the National Security Council in 2004, Pandith helped develop the “soft power” side of the Global War on Terror through a new approach called Countering Violent Extremism. Military action might disrupt extremist organizations, but it could not prevent them from recruiting new members. Nor were public relations campaigns successful in overcoming the distrust of Muslims worldwide. Even in her own government, distrust was impossible to ignore. One congressman called the White House to complain a “jihadist” was sitting in the Council. Weighed down by negative news? Enter your email below to receive our smart, uplifting newsletters. Or click here to choose exactly which ones you want [contact-form-7] Pandith was briefly living in Afghanistan’s capital, Kabul, in 2004 when photographs of abuse at Abu Ghraib surfaced showing American soldiers humiliating Muslim prisoners. “In an instant, all our efforts on the ground were harmed irreparably,” she says. Locals asked how she could represent a government that treated Muslim prisoners that way. The experience reinforced a lesson: Building trust also meant receiving criticism, sitting through uncomfortable conversations. Pandith carried that approach into her work at the State Department, where Hillary Clinton appointed her the first U.S. special representative to Muslim communities in 2009. Instead of treating Muslim populations as a single audience for American messages, she traveled widely, meeting people in homes, mosques and community settings to learn what mattered to them. “You have to go to the rural areas,” she says, aiming to support credible local voices that could offer alternatives to extremist narratives. Pandith herself has been shaped by a background that made her an ideal diplomat. She came to the U.S. from Kashmir as a baby with her mother, a pulmonologist and the medical director of a hospital. Pandith describes growing up in a highly educated Muslim family without experiencing discrimination. She remembers an America in which people of different faiths could live alongside one another, “with a synagogue, a church, a mosque and a temple in the same part of town.” Today, she admits, that harmonious coexistence feels nearly impossible. Her parents separated when she was 10, and her mother raised Pandith and her brother on her own. One of her greatest influences was her uncle, a heart surgeon. “I’ve held the hearts of different people in my hands,” he would tell her. “Always remember: There is no difference between the heart of a Muslim, a Jew, a Hindu or a Christian.” Pandith feels she carries “many identities” — an American, a woman, a Muslim and a foreign policy professional, among others. While traveling as Special Representative to Muslim Communities in the Obama administration, she said she had a “superpower” when speaking with Muslims. When she told them she was born in Srinagar in Kashmir, India, the atmosphere often changed. “Suddenly I’m like a sister to them.” Farah Pandith on a panel at the Milken Institute Asia Summit. Courtesy of Farah Pandith Her ability to forge connections would become one of her greatest professional assets. By chance, Barbara Bush, the wife of President George H.W. Bush, visited Smith College during Farah’s senior year. She was so impressed by a speech Pandith gave as student body president that she helped her secure her job at USAID after graduation. That was how the young woman began traveling around the world. Pandith’s work challenged conventional explanations of radicalization. Poverty and lack of education, she argued, could not explain why people embraced violent ideologies. Some of the 9/11 terrorists were well educated. Pandith pointed to a different cause she observed in Muslim communities: deep identity crises among young people who struggled to find their place in a rapidly changing world. She thinks of a young woman in Denmark whose Imam told her she wasn’t a Muslim if she didn’t cover her head. Or Mubin Shaikh in Canada, who went to Pakistan and Syria as a 19-year-old to fight alongside the jihadists and who now teaches security politics at the University of Ottawa. Pandith has seen firsthand that dialogue can change minds. ““It’s less interesting for the media than an extremist’s video, but the conversations we had affected people.” Her initiatives have sought to make dialogue a shared responsibility. Against Violent Extremism became the world’s first and only network of former extremists, launched by the U.S. Department of State, the Institute for Strategic Dialogue and Google. The “Hours Against Hate” campaign encouraged teenagers to spend an hour doing something for someone different from themselves. Millions participated. Sisters Against Violent Extremism connected mothers concerned about their children’s vulnerability to extremist recruitment. In a citizen-dialogue program, Pandith traveled through Europe with other Muslim Americans to share experiences and listen to local concerns. People had the chance to meet someone they might otherwise see only through stereotypes and to develop a relationship that complicated those assumptions. In her book How We Win , recently reissued, Pandith remains stubbornly optimistic: The fight against extremism can be won. Preventing people from being drawn into extremist movements requires intervening early and bringing together the people who can reach them — not just government officials, but business leaders, teachers, local communities and influencers whose networks, knowledge and credibility government agencies lack. “The fight against violent extremism is not going to be won solely by the efforts of government,” she argues. “We need businesses to step up as never before, for the public interest as well as their own.” She insists that this work cannot be dismissed as idealism or do-goodery but is “a matter of national security” — as important as the hard power of military force. Pandith emphasizes that the underlying lessons can be relevant for many communities. The same dynamics of exclusion and dehumanization can fuel hostility toward religious minorities, LGBTQ+ people and Asian communities, among others. Still, she admits that the strategies for countering violent extremism never fully came to fruition, often mired in bureaucracy. “Congress provided just 0.0138 percent of funding compared to the funding for the military,” she calculates. “We know what we need to do. We spent 25 years researching and exchanging strategies. But we left the field to the extremists.” Pandith sees the reality as a call to action: “We cannot just wring our hands and keep saying things are bad and things are difficult and somebody else’s problem. We need everybody.” Wait, you're not a member yet? Join the Reasons to be Cheerful community by supporting our nonprofit publication and giving what you can. Join Cancel anytime She now works outside government to advance another part of this agenda, as senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations , teaching countering violent extremism at Georgetown University, and as a Global Peace Laureate for the Muhammad Ali Center. She has been developing the Muhammad Ali Index on compassion . For Pandith, compassion is the capacity to recognize another person’s humanity even amid disagreement, and to resist the impulse to turn differences into a reason for contempt. “There isn’t a faith on planet Earth that doesn’t have compassion in it. And even if you are not religious you understand what it means, right?” As part of the Muhammed Ali Index, more than 5,400 people in 12 American cities responded to the 2025 State of Compassion survey . Sixty-one percent said they felt compassion has declined in the last four years, but 43 percent were optimistic about the future of compassion in America. A second index, planned for 2027, will cover 20 U.S. cities and 12 cities around the world. The ambition is practical. Pandith hopes the data will help mayors, school leaders, faith groups and local organizations identify opportunities to build stronger connections and design efforts suited to their own communities. The point is not to prescribe a universal program, but to create a framework that can be adapted. “We want to see people taking inspiration from the data to actually do something over time so we can measure and see what takes place,” she says passionately, insisting that compassion can be trained: “Compassion is a muscle that can be exercised.” Yet the starting point is personal: “Self-compassion is essential.” Building the capacity for compassion, Pandith argues, begins with recognizing what is happening inside oneself. She is particularly interested in reaching young people early. “The world that they are growing up in is so polarized and so difficult and so different from the one that we have grown up in,” she says, “that they don’t have a memory of people who are different from them speaking to each other with dignity regularly.” As Pandith sees it, waiting for polarization to disappear on its own is not a strategy. The task is to build relationships and connections that open up hearts and minds — and to keep investing in them long enough to learn what works. She repeats her favorite sentence: “Solutions are available and affordable.” UPDATE — November 3, 2026: This story has been updated to clarify facts about Pandith’s work and background. The post The Counter-Extremism Expert Building Our Capacity for Compassion appeared first on Reasons to be Cheerful .

items.descriptionOriginal: Some bees line their nests with soft petals. Some line them with hardened tree sap. Some line them with a thin, flexible film composed of silk and polyester. And this latter group—known as cellophane bees—may hold the key to sustainable, biodegradable plastic, according to a new study. “Nature has already solved a problem that polymer scientists are still working on: a bioplastic that is chemically and physically similar to conventional plastics but doesn’t persist in the environment,” says study team member Jonathan Coote , assistant professor in the Department of Sustainable Biomaterials at Virginia Tech University. Unlike more familiar hive-dwelling honeybees, cellophane bees nest in the soil. Females lay eggs in individual chambers that they line with secretions from a gland on their abdomen. Scientists have known for almost half a century that this lining is composed of silk fibers and a polyester similar to polyethylene—a material that makes up about one-third of human-produced plastics and is the most commonly used plastic for packaging. “Polyethylene-like polyesters made in the lab generally don’t break down well in the environment,” says Coote. “The bees’ material, however, breaks down rapidly in soil.” Although the bees nest in aggregations of 10,000 or more individual nests and often use the same nest sites for decades, their habitat never becomes choked with plastic—in contrast to large aggregations of modern humans. To find out more about how the bees do it, Coote and his collaborators gathered nest linings from two Tennessee nest sites of a species of cellophane bee known as Colletes inaequalis . They put the material through a battery of tests to characterize its structure and chemical makeup. They also collected nest linings that had been in the ground for four, seven, and 11 months to track how the material degrades over time. .IRPP_ruby , .IRPP_ruby .postImageUrl , .IRPP_ruby The tradeoff at the heart of bioplastics. A fresh nest cell lining is about 73% polyester and 27% silk by weight, the researchers report. The polyester is semicrystalline, likely has cross-linked polymer chains, and has a crystal structure and degradation temperature similar to that of polyethylene. “The biggest surprise was that the material is most likely cross-linked, meaning its polymer chains are chemically tied together into a network,” says Coote. “Cross-linked plastics, called thermosets, are typically very durable, and designing thermosets that break down at the end of their life is a major challenge in polymer science. So finding a thermoset that breaks down rapidly in soil was very counterintuitive, and it’s exciting to have a natural example to learn from.” By four months, the nest linings are just 40% polyester, meaning that the polyester degrades even more rapidly than famously biodegradable silk in the first months (after that, the composition changes much more slowly). Four-month-old nest linings remain flexible and intact, protecting the nest cell from moisture and microbes like a shrink-wrapped bell pepper at the grocery store. By seven months, about the time the larva has developed into an adult bee, the lining easily cracks easily; by 11 months, it crumbles in the hand. In other words, unlike that bell pepper’s shrink wrap, the nest lining lasts just as long as is needed to protect the developing bee, and no longer. The researchers next aim to investigate how the material breaks down so quickly. They hypothesize that the particularities of polyester’s crystal structure may leave the bonds that connect the material’s subunits exposed to a greater degree than in other polyesters. There’s also evidence of an enzyme that breaks these bonds present in the nest lining, perhaps from the mother bee’s saliva. “The goal is to reverse engineer what the bees are doing so that we can design similar materials in the lab and eventually produce them at practical scale,” Coote says. Source: Coote J.P., et al. “ Rapid soil degradation of a cross-linked, semicrystalline polyethylene-like polyester produced by Colletes bees .” PNAS 2026. Image: Laura Russo.

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News How Wildlife Conservation Filmmaking Turns Powerful Stories into Real-World Action Reading Time: 3 minutes Wildlife conservation filmmaking connects audiences with wild places and the people protecting them. Wildlife conservation filmmaking gives viewers a reason to care about wild places they may never see in person. Fin and Fur Films , an award-winning production company, builds its work around that idea. Its team focuses on wildlife, adventure, and conservation stories. The company says it is proudest of films that led to real-world conservation impacts. That goal shapes every project. In wildlife conservation filmmaking, a film succeeds when it moves audiences to care, not just when it entertains. Ben Masters, founder and director, started the company in 2012 with a Kickstarter campaign. Kickstarter is an online fundraising platform where many people donate small amounts. That campaign paid for the film Unbranded. Unbranded follows four young cowboys who adopted, trained, and rode a string of wild mustangs 3,000 miles from Mexico to Canada. That is about the distance across the continental United States. The route crossed some of the wildest terrain in the American West. The trip included runaway horses, a sassy donkey, perilous mountain passes, and rodeos. It also brought sickness, injury, and death. The film won the Audience Award at Telluride Mountainfilm and the Hot Docs Film Festival. Unbranded also shines a light on the complex situation facing the country’s wild horses. The adventure holds attention, and the film explains the issue along the way. Wildlife conservation filmmaking often works this way. The River and the Wall takes a similar approach. Five friends travel 1,200 miles from El Paso to the Gulf of Mexico through the unknown wilds of the Texas borderlands. They go by horse, mountain bike, and canoe. That distance equals nearly a full day of nonstop highway driving, but the friends covered it much more slowly. They set out to document the borderlands. They also wanted to explore how a border wall could affect the natural environment. As the wilderness gave way to the more populated Lower Rio Grande Valley, the friends met the human side of the immigration debate. The trip took an emotional turn they had not planned for. Deep in the Heart: A Texas Wildlife Story brings wildlife conservation filmmaking to an entire state. Actor Matthew McConaughey narrates the visually stunning film. It celebrates Texas landscapes and wildlife found nowhere else. Wildlife conservation filmmaking comes to an entire state in Deep in the Heart: A Texas Wildlife Story , narrated by Matthew McConaughey, a visually stunning film celebrating Texas landscapes and wildlife found nowhere else. Photo courtesy of Fin and Fur Films . The film aims to protect the state’s remaining wild places. It shows how water and wildlife depend on each other. It also recognizes Texas’s important role in conservation across the continent. Reach matters in wildlife conservation filmmaking. Fin and Fur Films has shared its work through Netflix, Apple TV, PBS Nature, Prime, National Geographic, and LoveNature. The films have also appeared in large theatrical releases and on international television. Global Wildlife Conservation notes that well-made environmental documentaries can bring people closer to nature and inspire them to protect it. The Fin and Fur Films catalog shows how that works in practice. Each story pairs a real adventure with a real conservation question. Partnerships help wildlife conservation filmmaking go further. The company has worked with American Rivers, The Nature Conservancy, and Texan by Nature. It has also partnered with brands such as H-E-B and YETI. The numbers show how far a small team can stretch. The company has produced five feature films and more than 30 short films. It has worked with more than 40 conservation groups, which is roughly one partner group per film. See also: A Documentary About Overfishing Sparked Blue Marine Foundation’s Ocean Conservation Mission Masters says the crew keeps its roots as river lovers, backcountry horsemen, and field-savvy wildlife biologists. He also stresses that each film is a team effort. Dozens, or even hundreds, of people contribute to each one. Masters credits partners, collaborators, donors, contractors, and the viewers who give their time to watch. That shared support keeps the work going. Audiences are part of the effort, too. Good stories make conservation feel personal. Wildlife conservation filmmaking gives those stories a wide audience. Which wild place would you most like to see protected next? The post How Wildlife Conservation Filmmaking Turns Powerful Stories into Real-World Action appeared first on Happy Eco News .
