Και σίγουρα, τα τρόφιμα που εκπέμπουν περισσότερο άνθρακα είναι επίσης αυτά που τείνουν να είναι τα χειρότερα για την υγεία μας, όπως τα κρέατα και τα γαλακτοκομικά. Τι θα γινόταν, λοιπόν, αν προσπαθούσαμε να φορολογήσουμε αυτόν τον άνθρακα, να ωθήσουμε τους ανθρώπους σε δίαιτες υψηλότερων φυτών που είναι πιο υγιεινές για τους ανθρώπους και τον πλανήτη; Μια νέα μελέτη στο Nature Food…
items.descriptionOriginal: Food accounts for a third of humanity’s greenhouse emissions. And sure enough, the most carbon-gushing foods are also the ones that tend to be the worst for our health, such as meats and dairy. So what if we tried taxing that carbon, to nudge people toward higher-plant diets that are healthier for people and planet alike? A new study in Nature Food explores how these food emissions taxes could be applied to countries around the world with different levels of wealth and greenhouse emissions. It shows how they could be tweaked to manage the delicate interplay between food prices, poverty, hunger, and health—while still cutting billions of tons of annual emissions. Economists have estimated that growing populations and increasing meat consumption worldwide could cause the environmental footprint of our food—including greenhouse emissions— to balloon by 50 to 90 percent by 2050 . This has spurred recommendations that humanity shift its diet , toward fewer animals and more plants. Emissions taxes paid by consumers buying foods are one way to encourage a shift away from meats, dairy, eggs , and sugars . But questions remain about how those taxes can be applied fairly to countries around the world—given that wealthier nations have more ability to pay them, and that many of these same nations also contributed disproportionately to rising greenhouse gases in the first place. In the new study, researchers used economic, trade, and public health models to predict how well different types of taxes would curb greenhouse emissions—and also, how they would impact food prices They compared two tax scenarios. In one, emissions are priced the same worldwide, at a constant cost of USD$ 185 per metric ton of CO 2 equivalent (tCO 2 eq). In this system, wealthy countries would still pay more taxes, because their food systems emit more tons of CO 2 . In the other system, the cost-per-ton of emissions is scaled up or down, based on each country’s wealth—thereby further increasing the taxes paid by consumers in wealthy countries (to as much as $969 per tCO 2 eq), while reducing those paid by lower-wealth countries (to as little as $21 per tCO 2 eq). The researchers compared these two scenarios both with and without a second provision, in which governments would also subsidize fruits and vegetables to further lower the prices that consumers pay for these low-carbon foods. Their results suggest that taxes based on a fixed-price-per-ton would reduce food-related emissions most sharply—by up to 18.7 percent, or about 2.6 billion tCO 2 eq worldwide each year. But such taxes would likely worsen overall health in some countries such as India, Bangladesh, and Vietnam—even after accounting for reductions in heart disease and diabetes—because they might make food less affordable to some people, compromising nutrition. The authors found that adjusting the price-per-ton of emissions based on national wealth would lessen this problem. And subsidizing the cost of fruits and vegetables would further decrease it. Together these two tweaks slightly reduced the emissions that were prevented—but they were still predicted to cut worldwide food emissions by 17 percent, or about 2.3 billion tCO 2 eq per year. The authors recommended that these efforts to reduce the negative impacts on the poor could be further explored, with detailed studies of poverty in individual countries, and potentially by excluding some critical sustenance foods such as fish or rice from the taxes in some countries. Bouyssou, et al. “ Food emissions taxes can deliver health and environmental benefits with limited leakage .” Nature Food , 2026. Image: ©Anthropocene Magazine

items.title: Αλήθεια, Εκλογές και Αμφισβητήσιμη Ιστορία του Club Sandwich
items.titleOriginal: Truth, Elections and the Questionable History of the Club Sandwich

Εάν ο στόχος σας είναι να μεταφέρετε λαθραία ανακρίβεια στην εγκυκλοπαίδεια του Διαδικτύου, μαθαίνετε γρήγορα να αφήνετε τα γνωστά πράγματα με τα σκληρά και γρήγορα γεγονότα μόνοι. Προσπαθήστε να αλλάξετε τη μάχη του Hastings t…
items.descriptionOriginal: I n the early-ish days of Wikipedia, my college friends and I had an ongoing contest to see who could introduce a lie into an entry that would stick the longest. If your goal is to smuggle mistruth into the internet’s encyclopedia, you quickly learn to leave the well-known stuff with hard-and-fast facts alone. Try to change the Battle of Hastings to 1068, or claim Thomas Jefferson wrote Flowers for Algernon , and the Wiki editors swoop in to excise your lies within minutes. It was oddly inspiring to see that the online compulsion to be right, and for things to be right, could become a kind of immune system for upholding the truth. Observing the editors’ behaviors, I conjured up a new strategy. I found a less-trafficked page — the entry for club sandwich — and located a sentence that was already conjecture, and which notably had a citation affixed to its end. The line read: It is thought that the club sandwich was invented in an exclusive Saratoga Springs, New York gambling club in the late 19th Century. I changed this by adding my buddy Danny as the sandwich’s inventor: It is thought that the club sandwich was invented in an exclusive Saratoga Springs, New York gambling club in the late 19th Century by a maverick line cook named Danny Mears. It’s unlikely that John McPhee had stumbled across our Wikipedia sandwich lie when he wrote that “any error is everlasting” in his 2009 New Yorker piece about the magazine’s fact-checking department. But he was right. “Maverick line cook Danny Mears” hardened into sturdier fiction with each repetition, appearing in poorly researched blog posts and online recipes, each mention making the lie seem more true. Wiki editors pulled it down a few times; we snuck it back in. In the end, Mears’ reign as the sandwich’s inventor persisted on Wikipedia for more than three-and-a-half years. An annoyed editor even added a Wiki “talk” comment exposing our misdeeds, titled Danny Mears Did Not Invent It . A couple years later, a friend texted the group to say she’d seen “maverick line cook Danny Mears” go up on the flatscreens as a bar-trivia answer. McPhee goes on to describe the job of fact-checking as a kind of noble guardian, holding back a teeming horde of mistruths: “With drawn sword, the fact-checker stands near the end of this bridge.” We’d camouflaged our lie past a few of these sentries for what amounted to a joyride, but eventually the guards got us. What I’ve been wondering ever since, and especially lately, is: Who’s still guarding that bridge? O ne may initially concede that our defenses seem to be diminishing in the present moment. You don’t have to look far to find a commentator mourning a “post-fact” world or worrying that we swim in toxic waters online when it comes to bad actors and misinformation. Consider that 20 percent of Americans surveyed by Pew Research said they regularly get their news from TikTok, up from three percent in 2020. Last year, Meta ended its U.S. fact-checking program, while the courts have decided that social media platforms are private providers of forums for speech and so can set their own content rules, or remove the guardians from the bridge entirely, depending on their business incentives. Credit: patpitchaya / Shutterstock There are few forces more powerful in the media than a stubborn person on the phone investigating a doubt. In the public sphere of reportage, Duke Reporters’ Lab, which has tracked fact-checking trends for years, found that last year was the first time fact-checking department closures outpaced launches . And on the level of the individual, three-fourths of the fact-checkers surveyed by the International Fact-Checking Network reported being financially vulnerable or in crisis . If the field has had a famous debunker in the last two decades, it has been t he Washington Post ’s Glenn Kessler, who last year accepted a buyout and was not replaced. Should you want to pre-write a eulogy for the capital-T Truth, the material is all here. But fact-checking is not a static field. Like our immune systems, it’s capable of learning and enduring, as well as mobilizing to handle infections of mistruth, which if not treated tend to further polarize voters in political contests. Consider recent false claims from his opponents that Texas Senate candidate James Talarico had disappeared from the campaign trail for mental health treatment at an inpatient facility in Ohio. A high-profile fact-check quickly shifted the narrative from “Talarico is in trouble” to “his opponents look like liars.” (Talarico had the flu and was resting at home, which the New York Times proved by reviewing security camera footage.) Bad-faith punditry has a lessened effect when met with undeniable facts and data, as do the rumors that chip away at our trust in elections themselves. Consider a recent viral video in which a woman from Cook County, Illinois claimed that her voting machine was telling her that her chosen candidate was the less-popular choice. Nonpartisan fact-checks from places like PolitiFact quickly rushed to explain the less-salacious reality: She hadn’t selected enough candidates. Fact-checks can bring the temperature down and reduce our polarization; her town’s Republican Committeeman even rose to refute the claims on Facebook . So while the institutional layer of the media is wounded and we’re ushering in an age of slop and lies, any obituary for the Truth is likely premature. Weighed down by negative news? Enter your email below to receive our smart, uplifting newsletters. Or click here to choose exactly which ones you want [contact-form-7] “Ever since I was a little kid, I’ve had a thing about wanting to get stuff right,” says Jy Murphy, a freelance fact-checker for the Hearst stable of publications and others. “At this point it bleeds over as a kind of professional deformity.” Murphy tells a simple story set years ago, in which he was fact-checking a Popular Mechanics piece about the freight industry and encountered a confident sentence claiming that nobody double-stacks rail cars in the Eastern U.S. because the bridges were all built with too little clearance. Fact-checkers encounter these offhand assertions all the time: a just-so statement with the ring of a thing that everybody knows. If you were to Google this type of niche knowledge, you might not find anything, and so the fact-checker operates most often as a reporter of the reporting. But after calling the railroad lines themselves, Murphy learned that in the year since the writer had filed the piece, a considerable number of bridges had been raised to allow freight through. The writer’s claim was “either too pessimistic to begin with or had changed in that year,” says Murphy. There are few forces more powerful in the media than a stubborn person on the phone investigating a doubt. It is precisely that thoroughness that makes peer-to-peer fact-checking matter more now in the age of A.I. Of course most large language models (LLMs) can’t yet make phone calls to freight lines, but if I ask Claude about Murphy’s rail bridges I may well still be told that nobody double-stacks rail cars in the Eastern U.S. That model can create a convincing, seemingly well-sourced sentence in a few seconds, but what it is not doing is actually checking the fact . Kelsey Lannin, a Seattle-based fact-checker, tells me that A.I is “very good at aping a confident intellectual on any given topic. But do any amount of work with it and you’ll quickly realize it’s a facade.” She says that it’s better to look at it like having an intern: “You give it an assignment, it gives you something back, and you [still] have to check it.” A.I. boosters may tell you that we’re just getting started, and assure us that this is the worst A.I. will ever be. Nevertheless, A.I. is still failing to produce accurate citations in more than 60 percent of tests, according to a 2025 Tow Center study . Prominent critics say it has nuked the effectiveness of Google and is “ destroying search, the internet and your brain. ” Models create a texture of verification, but they aren’t doing the analog process that makes verification real. If you see a bird out of your window, you can grab an Audubon guide and verify it. Feed a picture of that bird to an LLM and that model is neither “seeing” the chickadee nor “reading” from a primary source specifically. Models produce the most statistically likely next words, but unless prompted, there isn’t a step where Claude or Gemini confirms the truth of its response against the truth of the world. Credit: Andrey_Popov / Shutterstock Fact-checking’s collective response to changing times will continue to be a necessary governor, helping pace our accelerated information environment and dismantle false narratives that fuel polarization. These individual hallucinations and absent citations might seem like drops in a bucket, but they add up to create a rising tide of mistrust in a society already wary of the truthfulness of mainstream media . “What grieves me,” says Murphy, “is how many people think there aren’t [trusted sources].” Still, it is encouraging to see the fact-checking infrastructure responding by adapting to, and building defenses against, this flood. Sometimes, resistance looks like digging in. Inside the same Reporters’ Lab census that tallied closures, we learn that we’ve still got 437 active fact-checking projects around the world, which is just 27 below the all-time high and more than were operating in 2020. Many American newsrooms (North Dakota News Cooperative, CT Mirror in Connecticut and more) have agreed to work with Gigafact , an organization that publishes independently verified “fact briefs.” Wikipedia adopted a stronger A.I.-generated content policy earlier this year, banning LLM-generated content on the site, bar in certain circumstances. And as something becomes perceived to be scarce, it also becomes valuable: A 2026 Reuters study points toward an “increased demand for verification” from readers in a low-trust environment. The most encouraging turn of resistance may be in redirecting the machine back at the onslaught itself. Full Fact , the U.K.’s independent fact-checking charity, is now using A.I. systems to “detect and classify claims across millions of sentences,” per Reuters . A newer version attempts to “prebunk” instead of debunk, creating a model that prioritizes the most potentially damaging narratives for review. A Joint Research Centre study published in Nature investigated and concluded that debunking and prebunking interventions were successful and effective in reducing misinformation’s threats. Like any effort in inoculation, this effort will also need to be collective. At the end of last year, Scott Klein, then-publisher advocate at Newspack, predicted a “return to prioritizing open source collaboration, not as a luxury but as an existential imperative,” highlighting the need for a “show your work” ethos that will help journalism rebuild trust. Full Fact’s tools are being used now by more than 40 organizations across 30 countries, and importantly, the effort is mostly triage. Full Fact offers that the organization will “always keep human experts in the loop, partly to minimise the risks around bias and hallucinations that come with fully-automated systems but mostly because even the most advanced A.I. does not come close to human reasoning.” Wait, you're not a member yet? Read broadly and try to identify common threads.” Bringing the fact-checker’s stubborn doubt to our daily engagement is available to anyone willing to take a minute before they share a post. Years after my Wikipedia crime spree, I’m heartened that there are fact-checkers out there guarding the bridge and encouraged by the durability of this work. Reports of the Truth’s demise have perhaps been greatly exaggerated. It can be slow and unglamorous, but fact-checking’s collective response to changing times will continue to be a necessary governor, helping pace our accelerated information environment and dismantle false narratives that fuel polarization. “There are,” says Murphy, “good soldiers … a cadre of us out there trying to fight the good fight.” The post Truth, Elections and the Questionable History of the Club Sandwich appeared first on Reasons to be Cheerful .
